proposals.name: Definite localization of the asker's specific error
proposals.instruction: Score how precisely and how confidently the answer pins the exact place where the asker's own shown work goes wrong. 10 = the answer identifies a specific line, sign, term, or step in the asker's attempt, states flatly that it is wrong, and gives the corrected expression in place (e.g. 'you are correct except one sign, it should be ...', 'you got to here correctly but the line beneath is not'). 5 = the answer engages the attempt but only gestures at the region of the mistake, or corrects silently without saying where the asker went wrong. 0 = the answer either ignores the asker's attempt entirely, or only speculates about it in hedged terms ('I suppose that your mistake is ...') without committing to a located, corrected step. Judge only the definiteness and specificity of the localization, not whether the correction is right.
proposals.rationale: R51 and R58 both consist almost entirely of a pinpoint correction to the asker's own algebra ('you just made a little arithmetic mistake near the end', 'you are correct except one sign'), and R21 does the same for a mis-taken derivative; R09 locates a quantifier slip in a proof the asker wrote. A criterion bank built around self-contained mathematical content will read these as thin, because the mathematics they add is tiny. The contrast case is R32, which does address the asker's work but only as a hedged guess ('I suppose that your mistake is'), and R23, which re-solves from scratch without ever touching the asker's route.

proposals.name: Minimal unlocking hint that stops at the pivot
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer isolates the single idea that makes the problem tractable and then deliberately stops, rather than either grinding out routine steps or stopping short of any pivot. 10 = the answer delivers one decisive move (a substitution, a completed square, a named lemma, a reordering of the goal) that visibly collapses the difficulty, and ends there or almost there. 5 = the answer contains a real pivot but buries it inside mechanical work of comparable length. 0 = the answer offers no pivot at all, only routine execution that any competent reader would have produced unaided, or a fragment that stops before reaching anything decisive. Length alone is not the criterion: a short answer with no pivot scores low.
proposals.rationale: R02 (complete the square, then the digit sum), R37 (partial-fraction the trigonometric kernel, then one substitution), R20 (three-step ladder for the Boolean ordering) and R08 (look at the series, ask which terms survive at zero) are all very short and all hand over exactly the unlocking move. An explicit-criteria bank tends to reward exposition, coverage and completeness, all of which these forgo. R19 and R55, by contrast, execute long routine procedures (a textbook u-substitution; four separate evaluations of a linear map on a basis) with no pivot to isolate.

proposals.name: Insight density: distinct ideas per unit of length
proposals.instruction: Estimate how many genuinely distinct mathematical ideas the answer contains, then judge that count against its physical length. 10 = nearly every line carries a new idea, condition, or step that could not be predicted from the previous line; nothing is expanded for ceremony. 5 = the answer has a solid core of ideas surrounded by a comparable bulk of mechanical expansion, re-statement, or display formatting. 0 = the answer is long relative to its idea content: large displays, enumerated cases, or repeated parallel computations that instantiate one idea many times. Do not reward brevity as such; a short answer that also contains no ideas scores in the middle-low range, not high.
proposals.rationale: R33 resolves the whole question in two lines (difference of squares plus a divisibility caveat) and R45 in a single chained inequality. Against them, R24 devotes an enormous cofactor-matrix display to what reduces to one identity, and R55 repeats the same substitution four times over, while R43 restates the same parity argument in several registers. An explicit-criteria bank scoring thoroughness, structure and presentation will credit exactly the bulk that this criterion discounts, which is the shape of the R24 / R55 / R43 disagreements.

proposals.name: Written to this asker rather than to a general reader
proposals.instruction: Score the degree to which the answer is oriented to the particular person who asked, as opposed to being a general exposition that happens to be posted here. 10 = sustained second-person address that tracks what this asker appears to know, believe, or have tried ('you seem to be confused between X and Y', 'when you write ..., you have taken arbitrary elements in both'). 5 = occasional second-person framing over otherwise generic exposition. 0 = purely third-person exposition of the mathematics, with no trace of who asked or what they were stuck on. Judge orientation only, not correctness or tone.
proposals.rationale: R22, the most extreme dense-high item in the slice, is almost entirely a diagnosis of what this asker believes ('you seem to be greatly confused on a couple of concepts', 'let me dispel that confusion'); R09, R46 and R16 are likewise addressed to a specific attempt or specific puzzlement. The dense-low side is dominated by impersonal expositions: R12, R24, R30 and R36 could each be dropped into a textbook unchanged. A bank of content criteria has no natural slot for addressee-orientation, so it scores the textbook prose higher.

proposals.name: Authoritative candor versus apologetic self-hedging
proposals.instruction: Both high and low ends involve the author talking about their own answer; distinguish the stance. 10 = candid asides delivered from command of the material: flagging that one's own displayed manipulation is invalid, calling a standard technique obsolete, offering suggestions while stating plainly that they may not help. The author's authority is not in question; only the material or the approach is being appraised. 0 = hedging about the author's own competence or effort: 'I think I have the answer', 'I'm not sure you can do better', unexplained tentativeness about whether the claim is even true, or asking readers to repair the post. 5 = no self-reference either way.
proposals.rationale: R39 leaves 'edit: And well, this is broken' attached to its own derivation, R59 volunteers that stem-and-leaf plots are pointless to teach, and R60 offers three routes with 'no promise that they will be helpful' -- all confident appraisals, all dense-high. The opposite posture runs through the dense-low side: R35 opens 'I think I have the answer', R57 'I think the statement is false', R17 'I'm not sure you can do better', and R31 closes by asking someone to fix its TeX. A judge scoring hedging as a single signed feature will get this backwards, which is likely part of why the two models split on R39 and R31.

proposals.name: Names a result that immediately settles the question
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer supplies a named theorem, isomorphism, or classification that does the actual work of resolving the question, as opposed to naming things for context. 10 = a named result is invoked and the question collapses under it in a sentence or two ('the function satisfies the conditions of Clairaut's theorem, so no such function exists'; 'G/Z(G) is isomorphic to Inn(G)'; 'this group is D6 and we know all subgroups of dihedral groups'). 5 = a named result is invoked but substantial work remains and is not shown. 0 = no named result, or a name is supplied purely as decoration or trivia while the answer's real argument proceeds independently of it.
proposals.rationale: R07 opens by settling the existence question with Clairaut before offering a direct argument as a bonus; R41 and R56 are one-line answers that consist entirely of the reframing name; R27 settles a relative-homology computation with 'Z is free, so the sequence splits'. The decorative case is R31, which names the director circle and the Fermat-Apollonius circle 'for the sake of interest' and then proves everything from scratch, and R44, which attaches 'order statistics' as a label after the fact. A criterion bank that credits citation of standard results will treat these identically; the load-bearing versus decorative distinction is what separates them.

proposals.name: Repairs the misconception generating the question
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer identifies and dismantles the underlying confusion that produced the question, rather than only supplying the requested object. 10 = the answer names the two things the asker is conflating, defines each separately, and shows why the conflation caused the difficulty. 5 = the answer resolves the literal question and gestures at a conceptual moral. 0 = the answer supplies the requested object with no diagnosis, or misses that a conceptual confusion is present at all. This can be scored on any answer: if no misconception is discernible in the question, score by whether the answer nonetheless makes the governing concept explicit.
proposals.rationale: R22 separates 'spanning set of V' from 'span of a subset' before touching the theorem, and R09 isolates the exact logical distinction ('an arbitrary y in the image, which by definition equals phi(x) for some x') that the asker missed. R59 treats a stem-and-leaf question as a question about how to read the display at all, and R29 addresses why equipotence of a set and a proper subset feels wrong rather than proving it. All four are dense-high with low card scores, suggesting the bank credits delivered mathematics and not diagnosis.

proposals.name: Hypotheses guarded exactly where they bite
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer attaches side conditions and domain caveats at the precise point in the argument where they are needed. 10 = conditions appear inline and are load-bearing ('if a+b is nonzero, you can divide'; 'with the final inequality assuming n greater than 1'; a stated region of convergence that is narrower than the reader would assume). 0 = the argument uses an unstated hypothesis, asserts a necessary-and-sufficient condition without the qualifications it requires, or uses a term loosely in a way that would mislead a careful reader. 5 = conditions are correct but stated only in a blanket preamble, or the argument simply never needs one.
proposals.rationale: R33 and R45 are two-line answers whose only ornamentation is a precisely placed caveat, and R05 exists entirely to supply the caveat that a re-centred power series has a different region of convergence -- all dense-high. On the other side, R01 slides from grid counts to 'rational numbers' where it means real, R10 announces a necessary-and-sufficient condition for convexity of a product and then hedges it with 'a quick test', and R04 argues from 'their sum is 0 mod 3' when the needed statement concerns all integer combinations. These are exactly the kinds of local imprecision that a per-criterion bank scoring rigor at the whole-answer level will average away.

proposals.name: Continues the asker's chosen method instead of replacing it
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer picks up the route the asker had already started and carries it forward, versus discarding it for the answerer's preferred route. 10 = the answer explicitly adopts the asker's setup ('if, as you did, w = e^{iz}, then your equation becomes ...') and advances from there. 5 = the answer offers a different route but explains how it relates to what the asker tried. 0 = the answer solves the problem by an unrelated method with no acknowledgement that the asker had a method, or presents heavier machinery in place of the asker's elementary route. If the question shows no attempt, score by whether the answer works within the framework the question establishes.
proposals.rationale: R11 begins by adopting the asker's substitution verbatim and finishes it; R51, R58 and R21 all advance the asker's own computation rather than restarting. Against these, R23 re-derives a range from scratch in compressed algebra rather than engaging the asker's decomposition, and R54 replaces a routine partial derivative with formal composition notation the asker did not use. This is a distinct axis from error localization: an answer can locate an error and still throw the method away.

proposals.name: Closes the loop, or makes the remainder explicitly mechanical
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer terminates at a point the asker can actually use. 10 = the requested object is produced (a numeric answer, a closed form, an interval), or the residual step is named and is genuinely mechanical ('I leave it to you to simplify this expression', where only simplification remains). 5 = the answer reaches a correct but unevaluated expression and does not say what to do with it. 0 = the answer stops mid-thought, trails into a truncated addendum, or leaves the reader at a point where the hard part is still ahead and unnamed.
proposals.rationale: R02 ends with 'Answer: 13' and R14 produces the actual digits before handing off; R48 stops at a sum but names simplification as all that remains. Compare R03, which produces an unevaluated infinite sum as its entire content with no indication of how to evaluate it, and R25, which runs long and then breaks off inside a truncated 'EDIT' about Kummer-Dedekind. The distinction between a mechanical remainder and an unnamed hard remainder is invisible to a criterion that only asks whether a final answer is present.

proposals.name: Names the reader's next move precisely
proposals.instruction: Score how precisely the answer specifies what the reader should do next. 10 = the next action is a specific, checkable task ('now figure out when it becomes periodic'; 'show that x <= y implies x meet a <= y meet a'; 'which terms are those?'), so the reader knows both what to do and how they will know they have done it. 5 = a vague invitation to continue ('proceed similarly', 'the other case is analogous') without saying what similarity to exploit. 0 = no handoff, or a handoff to something as hard as the original problem.
proposals.rationale: R14 works the decimal expansion far enough to expose the pattern and then names the exact remaining question; R20 decomposes a Boolean-ordering proof into three checkable sub-claims; R08 ends on a question with a determinate answer. All three are short and dense-high with card scores below 0.35. This is a different property from A02: a hint can isolate the pivot without specifying what the reader is to do, and a handoff can be precise without being the pivot.

proposals.name: Register and typographic discipline
proposals.instruction: Score the surface craft of the post as a piece of mathematical writing. 10 = standard written prose, mathematics set in properly rendered notation, displays aligned and readable, no chat abbreviations, no maintenance requests directed at other readers. 5 = generally clean with isolated lapses. 0 = texting abbreviations in place of words, mathematics typed as raw ASCII where the surrounding corpus uses typeset notation, mangled or unrendered displays, or an explicit plea for someone else to fix the formatting. Judge presentation only; a well-presented wrong answer still scores high here.
proposals.rationale: R18 writes 'U have n black and n white balls' and 'U want to choose n balls'; R31 closes with a parenthetical asking someone to fix its TeX; R53's entire content is the ASCII string 'F(t)=(t^(3/2),0,0)' with no typesetting or verification. All three are dense-low with card scores from 0.60 to 0.92, so the bank is clearly not penalizing surface register. The comparison that isolates this is R18 against R48: the same question, a comparable counting argument, and R48's clean prose sits at the top of the dense distribution while R18 sits near the bottom.

proposals.name: Standalone contribution versus supplement to another post
proposals.instruction: Score how far the answer's value depends on other content in the thread. 10 = fully standalone; a reader who saw only this post would get a complete line of reasoning. 5 = standalone in substance but with a courtesy nod to another poster, or an acknowledged overlap that is then extended into something new. 0 = the post is framed as an extension, correction, or commentary on another answer ('to expand on X's answer', 'as was pointed out in another answer', a critique of a named user's use of a theorem) such that its content presupposes that other post.
proposals.rationale: R38 opens 'To expand on Stephen's answer', R13 opens by deferring to another answer for the counterexample, and R49 is largely an argument about whether another user's invocation of Lowenheim-Skolem is justified; all three are dense-low with card scores from 0.69 to 0.83. R15 is the informative middle case: it admits it has repeated a commenter but then supplies a general construction, and it lands dense-high. A bank judging each post in isolation cannot see this dependence at all, which makes it a plausible source of over-crediting.

proposals.name: Machinery calibrated to the question's level
proposals.instruction: Score the fit between the apparatus the answer deploys and the difficulty of the question. 10 = the lightest apparatus that actually settles the question, pitched at the level the question is asked from (elementary factoring for an exponent-rules question; informal cardinality talk for a first encounter with equipotence). 0 = conspicuous mismatch in either direction: formal machinery imported to dress up a routine computation, an enormous symbolic display where a short identity suffices, or apparatus so far below the question that the real difficulty is untouched. 5 = apparatus is somewhat heavy or light but does not obstruct.
proposals.rationale: R16 answers an exponent-sign question by factoring out a single -1, and R29 meets a first-encounter cardinality question with deliberately informal language before naming the real subtlety; both dense-high with card below 0.20. The mismatch cases are dense-low: R54 wraps a routine partial derivative in composition notation and in doing so writes a chain-rule statement that double-counts the inner derivative, and R24 fills the screen with a full cofactor matrix to extract one 2-by-2 determinant identity. Explicit criteria rewarding rigor and formal presentation will score the mismatched answers up.

proposals.name: Example or counterexample that is actually verified
proposals.instruction: Score whether a concrete instance offered by the answer is carried far enough that the reader can check it. 10 = the example is exhibited and then worked: the relevant quantities are computed or the defining property is checked, so the reader sees it do the job (an analogous series re-expanded and its narrower interval exhibited; a formal system enlarged by a specific formula and the resulting theorem set described). 5 = a well-chosen example is exhibited with the verification sketched or left as obvious. 0 = an object is asserted to be an example with no computation, no checking, and no explanation of which property fails.
proposals.rationale: R05 does not merely assert that re-centring changes the region of convergence, it re-expands the geometric series about one half and displays the resulting interval; R15 constructs an explicit larger inductive set by adjoining a chosen non-theorem. Both dense-high. R53 names a curve and stops without computing either quantity the question asks about, and R40's counterexample is asserted to be non-weakly-convergent from unboundedness without connecting to the structure of the claim it refutes; both dense-low with card above 0.60, so the bank appears to credit the presence of a counterexample rather than its verification.

proposals.name: Bulk and exposition scale of the answer
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of sheer textual bulk in the answer, considering only size and not merit: total word count, number of separate paragraphs or steps, number of display-math blocks, and whether the answer runs past the point where a minimal reply would have stopped. 0 = a single short sentence or one bare formula with no surrounding prose; 5 = a few paragraphs with two or three displayed expressions; 10 = a long multi-section treatment with many displayed blocks, enumerated cases, and extended commentary. Count what is on the page. You must NOT judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the extra material is useful, or whether the answer is correct, complete or well written; a long wrong answer and a long right answer receive the same score.
proposals.rationale: Verbosity is a pure size proxy that separates the slice sharply and is available to any text model without touching the target construct. R52 and R59 are multi-screen expositions with sectioning and case enumeration, R53 and R13 likewise run for many paragraphs, while R34 is two lines of ASCII, R56 is a single sentence, and R29 is one identity plus a clause. Bulk tracks how much a writer chose to type, which is a habit of the writer, not evidence about how answers to the same question compared.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Non-standard orthography and chat-register spelling
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of non-standard written English and casual keyboard register visible in the answer: SMS-style abbreviations ('U' for 'you'), misspellings ('Simplier', 'independant', 'chosing'), lowercase first-person 'i', missing or doubled spaces around punctuation ('them up.If you'), inconsistent capitalisation, stray emoticons or parenthetical asides in a chatty tone, and article/agreement patterns typical of English as a second language. 0 = clean, conventionally edited standard English throughout; 5 = two or three noticeable slips; 10 = pervasive non-standard spelling, spacing and register. Count occurrences of the trace only. You must NOT judge whether the writing is good, whether the slips impede understanding, or whether the mathematics is right.
proposals.rationale: This is a pure writer-identity trace with no bearing on the target construct. R10 writes 'U have $n$ black' and 'Simplier', R48 writes 'You mixed them up.If you look' and 'firstly at', R07 writes 'independant', R11 closes with the emoticon ='( and a plea about TeX, and R34 is bare ASCII with no formatting conventions at all. A judge can count these without any access to how the answers compared.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's editing practice and first language

proposals.name: MathJax markup fluency and display-typesetting habit
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of practised, site-idiomatic mathematical typesetting in the answer, judged as habit and not as quality: use of display math ($$ ... $$) rather than inline math for substantial expressions; use of structured environments (align, matrix, pmatrix, vmatrix, cases); use of tag numbers, \color, \operatorname, \mathfrak, \mathscr, \Bbb or \mathbb, \sqrt[n], spacing macros; consistent wrapping of every symbol in math mode; and use of blockquote, list or bold sectioning. 0 = mathematics typed as plain ASCII or unformatted text with no macros; 5 = correct inline and some display math, no environments; 10 = heavy multi-environment typesetting with numbered equations, colour, custom macros and structured layout. Score only how much of this markup machinery is present. You must NOT judge whether the typesetting is attractive, whether it aids the reader, or whether the content is correct.
proposals.rationale: Markup fluency is the most visible residue of how many posts someone has written here, and a practised poster may also genuinely write better answers, so this is tagged mixed rather than pure nuisance. R59 uses align blocks, \color{blue} highlighting and blockquoted case headers; R53 builds nested pmatrix and vmatrix displays with \tag numbering; R23 uses \color{red} inside an align chain; by contrast R34 types 'F(t)=(t^(3/2),0,0)' with no math mode whatsoever and R13 writes its symbols as literal unicode in running prose.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format (accumulated posting habit on the site)

proposals.name: Second-person audit of the asker's own posted attempt
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the answer is addressed to the individual asker and works over that person's own posted attempt rather than over the problem from scratch: verdicts on the asker's work ('You did it correctly', 'That looks fine to me', 'You are correct except one sign', 'You mixed them up', 'This is wrong', 'your derivative for RHS is correct'), quotation of the asker's own lines or notation, localisation of where the asker's error begins, and instructions phrased as corrections to something the reader already wrote. 0 = the answer never refers to anything the reader has done and reads as a standalone exposition for any future reader; 5 = one passing reference to the asker's work amid otherwise standalone exposition; 10 = the whole answer is a line-by-line audit of the asker's submitted attempt and is unintelligible without it. Score only the presence of this addressed-to-the-asker framing. You must NOT judge whether the correction is right, kind, or helpful.
proposals.rationale: Whether an answer can be an attempt-audit is set by what the asker happened to post, not by the answer's own standing among sibling answers, yet an author who diagnoses a specific error may also genuinely be writing a better answer, hence mixed. R19 opens 'You did it correctly. You just made a little arithmetic mistake near the end'; R03 opens 'That looks fine to me'; R23 says 'You are correct except one sign' and marks the error in red; R48 opens 'You mixed them up'; R58 says 'Your derivative for RHS is correct, but the notation is bad'. R09 quotes the asker's own sentence back verbatim.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's relationship to the reader (writing for the asker versus for future searchers), and the presence of a posted attempt in the question

proposals.name: Hint mode: deliberate withholding of the completed solution
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the answer withholds the finish rather than carrying the work to a conclusion: an explicit 'Hint:' or 'HINT:' opener, a numbered ladder of sub-steps for the reader to perform ('Show that...', 'Apply (1) and (2)'), a closing interrogative aimed at the reader ('Which terms are that?', 'Does that make sense?', 'can you show that'), an explicit handoff ('I leave it you to simplify this expression', 'Now you have to figure out when it becomes periodic'), or a stated final substitution left unevaluated. 0 = the answer runs to a complete finished result with nothing left for the reader; 5 = mostly complete but ends with one open prompt; 10 = the answer is a bare hint or scaffold with the substantive work explicitly deferred. Score only how much is withheld and how explicitly. You must NOT judge whether withholding is pedagogically good, nor whether the hint points in the right direction.
proposals.rationale: Hint-mode is a house convention some regulars adopt and others never do; it is a stylistic dialect of the venue rather than the target construct, but the same practised-regular parent may also produce genuinely stronger posts, so mixed. R02, R17, R21, R30, R39, R49 and R55 all literally open with 'Hint:' or 'HINT:'; R44 closes 'I leave it you to simplify this expression'; R60 closes 'Now you have to figure out when it becomes periodic'; R25 closes 'Does that make sense?'. This clusters across both halves of the slice and is countable from the text alone.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format (site norms for handling homework-style questions)

proposals.name: Hedged first-person stance versus flat declarative assertion
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of epistemic hedging in the answer's voice: first-person uncertainty markers ('I think', 'I'm not sure', 'I would do something like that', 'I believe', 'no promise that they will be helpful', 'may not be optimal'), softening discourse openers ('Well', 'It is not quite clear', 'something like'), conditional framing of the author's own claims, and explicit confessions of incomplete knowledge. Score 0 when the answer is uniformly flat and declarative with no first-person qualification at all, 5 when there is one clear hedge in an otherwise assertive text, and 10 when hedging saturates the answer from the first clause onward. Score only the density of the hedging language. You must NOT judge whether the hedging is warranted, honest, or well calibrated, and you must NOT judge whether the assertions are true.
proposals.rationale: Willingness to assert without hedging is a register habit tied to seniority in the venue, visible in the text, and separable from the target construct; but a confident author may also genuinely know more, so mixed. R04 opens 'Well since $\cos(0)=1$ I'm not sure you can do better'; R08 opens 'I think the statement is false'; R37 opens 'I think I have the answer using generating functions'; R10 opens 'I would do something like that'; R43 opens 'I think you could divide it into some easier parts'. At the other pole R56 is the single flat sentence 'Yes. Since $\mathbb Z$ is free, the sequence splits', and R29 asserts an identity with no voice at all.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's standing and self-positioning on the site (a practised regular's willingness to be flatly declarative)

proposals.name: Post-hoc maintenance marks and meta-commentary about the post
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of visible after-the-fact editing and self-referential commentary about the post itself: explicit 'EDIT', 'edit:', 'P.S.', 'Note:', '2nd note:' markers; appended material that answers something raised after the original writing; commentary on the post's own history or on other users' reactions; requests for help with the post's formatting; self-deprecating remarks about the post; and closing pleasantries such as 'Hope this helps!'. 0 = the answer contains no marker of revision, no meta-comment on itself, and no sign-off; 5 = one such marker or a single sign-off; 10 = several revision markers plus running meta-commentary about the post and its reception. Score only the visible markers. You must NOT judge whether the edits improved the answer, whether the meta-commentary is charming, or whether the content is right.
proposals.rationale: These marks are the textual fingerprint of an unseen process that happened after posting, so they are downstream of attention the post received rather than of the answer's standing among siblings; but an edited answer may also have been genuinely improved, hence mixed. R12 ends 'Hope this helps!' followed by a truncated 'EDIT.' section; R22 has an 'EDIT: I have three suggestions'; R25 appends 'Edit: I wouldn't worry about it too much'; R47 appends 'edit: And well, this is broken.'; R24 appends a 'P.S :' narrating which users asked for more; R11 asks 'can somebody please fix up my TeX'; R13 carries 'Note:' and '2nd note:' paragraphs.
proposals.upstream_parent: post-publication process dynamics (comment-thread pressure and revision history)

proposals.name: Language presupposing that sibling answers already exist
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the answer's own wording presupposes that other answers or comments to the same question are already present: naming another answerer or user, phrases such as 'To expand on X's answer', 'As was pointed out in another answer', 'as mentioned before', 'this is nicely considered in the answer from ...', 'I see I've just repeated someone's comment', positioning itself as an alternative or supplement ('A worse way to prove this is...', 'For the sake of interest'), or engaging an argument that is not in the question text. 0 = the answer engages the raw question from scratch as if nothing had yet been said; 5 = one glancing phrase implying prior discussion; 10 = the answer is structured explicitly as a reply to or extension of another answer and cannot stand alone. Score only the presence of this presupposing language. You must NOT judge whether the supplement is valuable or whether the engagement is fair.
proposals.rationale: This is the MODE 3 fingerprint of arrival order: an answer written seventh reads differently from one written first, and arrival order is not the target construct, though a late answer that fills a real gap may also be genuinely preferred, so mixed. R20 opens 'To expand on Stephen's answer'; R57 opens 'As was pointed out in another answer, this is not true in general'; R31 argues about a claim 'in Ove Ahlman's answer'; R59 defers a case to 'the answer from @ErickWong'; R46 parenthesises '(I see I've just repeated Daniel Schepler's comment here.)'; R26 says 'As you noticed'. Note R44 and R10 answer the same question and R51 and R02 answer the same question, so ordering effects are live in this slice.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream (how many answers had already been posted when this one arrived)

proposals.name: Era-marked notation, markup vintage and venue conventions
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of vintage or off-convention presentation habits that mark an answer as belonging to an older or non-current stratum of the site's conventions: mathematics typed as literal unicode or plain characters in running prose rather than in math delimiters ('k≥2', '⇒', 'N-1'), ASCII exponent and function notation ('t^(3/2)', 'cot^{-1}' typed outside math mode), regionally or historically marked abbreviations ('hcf' rather than 'gcd'), quoted-string state names in prose ('on'/'off' with typographic quotes), subject matter tied to a bygone teaching practice discussed as such, and absence of the structural markup (lists, display blocks, blockquotes) that is now routine. 0 = fully current, uniformly delimited, structurally marked-up presentation; 5 = a mix of current markup with a few plain-text mathematical expressions; 10 = the whole answer uses out-of-convention plain-text mathematics and vocabulary. Score only the vintage of the surface conventions. You must NOT judge whether the conventions are better or worse, and you must NOT infer or state any date.
proposals.rationale: A second MODE 3 fingerprint, this one for position in the site's history rather than in the answer stream; era is unrelated to how an answer compared with its siblings, so pure nuisance. R13 types 'k≥2 ⇒ k' = N-k+1' as running unicode prose with quoted 'on'/'off' states and no display math; R34 types 'F(t)=(t^(3/2),0,0)' with no delimiters at all; R20 writes '{\rm hcf}(n,i)' rather than gcd; R25 discusses stem-and-leaf plots as an artefact of 'the days when you had to plot everything by hand'.
proposals.upstream_parent: the era of the site the post comes from (which generation of conventions the author was writing under)

proposals.name: Elementary-course register versus graduate-topic register
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how far the answer's own vocabulary and apparatus sit toward the advanced end of the scale, treating this purely as a register measurement: score near 0 when the answer works entirely in first-course material (arithmetic of exponents, partial fractions, basic substitution integrals, chain rule, elementary counting, stem-and-leaf plots) and its named objects would be familiar to a first-year student; score near 5 for standard undergraduate machinery (group quotients, linear maps, convergence tests, Fourier transforms); score near 10 when the answer routinely names graduate or research-level objects and results without explaining them (ramification and the different, integral closures, Riemann surfaces and branch cuts, relative homology, Löwenheim-Skolem, order statistics of a family, weak convergence in Hilbert space). Judge only the level of the vocabulary and objects invoked. You must NOT judge whether the answer is sophisticated in a praiseworthy sense, whether the level is appropriate to the question, or whether the mathematics is correct.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4 question-kind fingerprint: subject-matter level is a property of the thread the answer landed in, and it changes how many readers and how many rival answers a post meets, which is upstream of reception but is not the target construct; a specialist answer may also be genuinely stronger, so mixed. R14 ('any time you take an even power ... discard any factor of -1'), R29, R40 and R41 are first-course computations; R12 discusses tame and wild ramification with the different and index of orders, R52 glues sheets of a Riemann surface across branch cuts, R56 answers a Hatcher relative-homology exercise, and R31 argues from the Löwenheim-Skolem theorem. The register is legible in the answer text alone.
proposals.upstream_parent: the kind of question the answer is attached to (routine homework computation versus conceptual question that draws a crowd) and the size of the audience it attracts

proposals.name: Personalized correction of the asker's own work
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the answer pinpoints and fixes a specific step in the asker's own posted attempt/reasoning, rather than answering in the abstract. 10 = the answer quotes or paraphrases the asker's specific move, names exactly where it goes wrong, and repairs that exact step (e.g., 'you got to X correctly but the next line should be Y'). 0 = the answer is fully generic/self-contained and never references anything the asker specifically did or wrote.
proposals.rationale: R11 ('You did it correctly. You just made a little arithmetic mistake near the end... it should actually be...') and R19 ('The derivative of log(xy) is not quite right. You should have instead...') are dense_high_card_low; the dense model appears to reward this tight, personalized engagement with the asker's actual attempt that a scorecard reading only for topical correctness would miss.

proposals.name: Confident, declarative register vs. hedged phrasing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the confidence of the answer's voice. 10 = fully declarative, no hedge words ('I think', 'I suppose', 'maybe', 'probably'); the author states results as settled fact. 0 = the answer is laced with hedging language that signals the author's own uncertainty about the claim being made.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('I think the statement is false...') and R17 ('I suppose that your mistake is...') both hedge their central claim and are dense_low_card_high, while confident openers like R11 ('You did it correctly') and R36 ('That looks fine to me') sit dense_high_card_low -- suggesting the scorecard is not penalizing hedged delivery the way crowd voters seem to.

proposals.name: Socratic hint that leaves the final step to the reader
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on how much the answer is structured as a guided hint versus a fully worked-through solution. 10 = the answer gives the key idea/first move(s) and explicitly stops short, leaving the remaining computation or conclusion for the reader to finish. 0 = the answer carries the derivation all the way to a final boxed/stated result with nothing left to do.
proposals.rationale: R05 ('HINT: Work up to it in steps... Apply (1) and (2) twice to get the desired results'), R41 ('Hint: Look at the expanded form... Which terms are that?'), and R04 ('I leave it you to simplify this expression') are all dense_high_card_low, while fully carried-through derivations like R10 and R56 are dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Insight density relative to length
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the ratio of genuine mathematical insight to verbiage. 10 = a short answer that delivers the key trick/observation with almost no throat-clearing or restatement (high insight per line). 0 = long exposition padded with restated setup, redundant notation-juggling, or repeated intermediate steps that add length without new insight.
proposals.rationale: R07 (three sentences: 123 and 321 are both multiples of 3, so the sum can't be 1 mod 3) and R55 (a two-line algebraic identity answer) are terse and high-insight; contrast the much longer, step-padded R10 and R56, which are dense_low_card_high despite (or because of) their length.

proposals.name: Visible personality / editorializing asides
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the author's personal voice, opinion, or humor is visible in the answer, beyond the bare math. 10 = the answer includes an aside that expresses opinion, humor, or personal reaction to the problem/topic. 0 = the prose is flat and impersonal throughout, purely exposition.
proposals.rationale: R33 ('there's basically no reason to use them anymore. That we still teach them in intro statistics classes is kind of silly') and R47 ('this is a rather dangerous! way to wrap your mind around this') both editorialize and are dense_high_card_low; the scorecard, built from topic-relevant criteria, plausibly has no slot for authorial personality.

proposals.name: Explicit engagement with other answers/answerers on the thread
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the answer explicitly references, builds on, or corrects another specific answer or answerer on the same question (by name, quote, or clear paraphrase). 10 = the answer names or clearly quotes another answer and engages with it directly. 0 = the answer is written as if in isolation, no reference to other responses.
proposals.rationale: R13 critiques 'Ove Ahlman's answer' directly, R28 notes '(I see I've just repeated Daniel Schepler's comment here.)', and R48 opens 'As was pointed out in another answer, this is not true in general' -- a mixed set spanning both disagreement directions, showing this is a real recurring structural feature the scorecard likely never captures since it scores each answer as a standalone unit.

proposals.name: Concrete worked example over pure abstraction
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the answer grounds its point in a specific, concrete instance (a particular number, function, or curve) rather than staying entirely symbolic/general. 10 = the core of the answer is a single concrete example or numeric instantiation that makes the point vivid. 0 = the answer stays fully general/symbolic with no worked concrete instance.
proposals.rationale: R40 answers with one concrete curve, F(t)=(t^(3/2),0,0), and nothing else, and R58 grounds a general expression in the specific plug-in leading to 'Answer: 13'; both are dense_high_card_low, suggesting crowd voters reward a well-chosen concrete instance that a criteria-based judge may score lower for lacking generality or rigor.

proposals.name: Diagnoses the underlying conceptual confusion, not just the mechanical error
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the answer names and explains the conceptual misunderstanding behind an error, rather than just supplying the corrected formula/step. 10 = the answer explicitly identifies what concept the asker is conflating or missing and clarifies it. 0 = the answer only patches the mechanical mistake with no discussion of the underlying concept.
proposals.rationale: R59 ('You seem to be greatly confused on a couple of concepts: Spanning set of a vector space. The span of a subset...') explicitly separates and re-teaches two conflated concepts, and R26 diagnoses a similar confusion about 'differentiating' one language from another; both are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Intuitive / plain-language analogy grounding the formalism
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the answer offers an intuitive, non-technical way of understanding the object before or instead of pure formal notation. 10 = the answer leads with a plain-language analogy or intuitive picture (e.g., an everyday framing) that carries real explanatory weight. 0 = the answer is pure formal notation/derivation with no intuitive framing at all.
proposals.rationale: R37 offers 'An engineering explanation' of sampling density using grids of samples, and R50 frames entropy as 'the cost of encoding a specific distribution' via a messaging analogy; both are grounded in intuition, though they land on opposite sides of the disagreement (R37 dense_low_card_high, R50 also dense_low_card_high), suggesting the crowd does not reward intuitive framing as reliably as one might expect and it is worth measuring directly rather than assuming.

proposals.name: Visible self-acknowledged limits or incompleteness
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the answer explicitly flags its own gap, failure, or incompleteness rather than presenting itself as fully settled. 10 = the author openly notes a limitation, error, or open piece of their own answer. 0 = the answer presents its content as complete and correct with no self-flagged caveat.
proposals.rationale: R15 ends with 'edit: and well, this is broken' -- an explicit admission the derivation fails -- yet is dense_high_card_low (dense_pct=0.977); R32 repeatedly flags its own technique's limits ('This technique unfortunately doesn't work for 2...') and is dense_low_card_high. The visible self-awareness itself seems to correlate with what the dense model perceives, independent of whether the underlying math is airtight.

proposals.name: Clean closing resolution vs. trailing off unresolved
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the answer reaches an explicit final resolution/result. 10 = the answer closes with a clearly stated final answer or completed result. 0 = the answer trails off mid-derivation or mid-thought without stating the resolution, leaving the reader to finish alone with no explicit hint that this was intentional.
proposals.rationale: R09 ends 'Now you have to figure out when it becomes periodic' without ever finishing, and R32 trails off with 'Kummer-Dedekinds theorem gives an explicit description of the primes' and stops; both are dense_low_card_high, consistent with a scorecard crediting the visible effort/technical content while the dense model (and, plausibly, real voters) penalize a solution that never lands.

proposals.name: Opens by directly refuting the question's or a prior claim's premise
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the answer's opening move is a direct refutation ('this is false', 'this is wrong', 'the statement is not true') of the question's premise or of a claim already on the thread, as opposed to accepting the premise and proceeding to solve. 10 = the answer opens with an unambiguous refutation. 0 = the answer fully accepts the question as posed and proceeds constructively with no refutation.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('I think the statement is false'), R16 ('This is wrong'), R39 ('False'), and R48 ('this is not true in general') all open with blunt refutation and are all dense_low_card_high -- a striking four-item cluster suggesting the scorecard may be over-crediting confident counterexample/refutation answers relative to how the crowd actually receives them.

proposals.name: Explicit recap of relevant definitions before applying them
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the answer explicitly restates the relevant definition(s) before using them, as a didactic scaffold for the reader. 10 = the answer clearly writes out the definition(s) needed and then applies them. 0 = the answer assumes the reader already has the definitions in hand and jumps straight to manipulation/computation.
proposals.rationale: R59 explicitly restates both 'spanning set of a vector space' and 'the span of a subset' as formal definitions before using them, and R38 restates what the cycle notation 'g=(1,...,n)' means as a map before manipulating it; both instances are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Invites reader dialogue or explicitly requests feedback
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the answer directly addresses the reader with a question or request (e.g., asking if the explanation makes sense, or asking for help/correction from others). 10 = the answer ends with or contains an explicit question/request directed at the reader/community. 0 = the answer is a pure monologue with no direct address inviting a response.
proposals.rationale: R33 closes with 'Does that make sense?' and R25 closes with 'can somebody please fix up my TeX so the chunk equations is centred and aligned?' -- both open a dialogue with the reader rather than delivering a closed monologue, and both are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Formal/technical machinery calibrated to the question's apparent level
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the weight of formalism/machinery in the answer matches the apparent difficulty level signaled by the question. 10 = the level of technical apparatus (notation, cited theorems, generality) is well matched to what the question calls for -- neither overkill for a simple question nor underpowered for a hard one. 0 = a clear mismatch, such as heavy multi-step formal machinery deployed on a question that reads as elementary/homework-level, or a bare hand-wave on a question that clearly demands rigor.
proposals.rationale: R03 answers an elementary sign-of-exponent question with a matched, compact algebraic demonstration and is dense_high_card_low; R56, by contrast, deploys a full 3x3 cofactor-matrix inverse and multi-equation derivation for what reads as a similarly homework-level rotation-matrix question, and is dense_low_card_high -- suggesting the scorecard rewards visible machinery even when it overshoots what the question calls for.

proposals.name: Answer length/verbosity
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how long and multi-step the answer is -- from an extremely terse one- or two-line reply to a long, multi-section derivation with many displayed equations. Score only the extent of length/verbosity present; do not judge whether the length is appropriate, sufficient, or whether the content is good.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high/card-low items like R31 and R39 are long multi-paragraph derivations, while dense-low/card-high items like R32, R42, R51 are one or two lines; raw length can drive both models independent of within-question crowd preference, and could also correlate with genuine thoroughness, so it is tagged mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Display-math/formatting elaborateness
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much elaborate LaTeX formatting the answer uses -- multi-line aligned or matrix environments, color macros like \color{...}, explicit numbered-equation tags, or visual section dividers -- versus plain running text with little or no display math. Score only the extent of formatting elaborateness present, not whether the formatting is effective, tasteful, or whether the underlying math is correct.
proposals.rationale: R39 and R50 use heavy colored/aligned/matrix LaTeX apparatus while R32, R42, R56 are almost bare prose; this typographic density is a plausible confound for a scorecard rubric that rewards apparent rigor, though careful formatting can also track genuine care in exposition.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Direct second-person address to asker
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the answer speaks directly to 'you' the asker -- e.g. 'you did X', 'your mistake', 'you should have' -- as opposed to writing in an impersonal third-person voice addressed to a general reader. Score only the extent of this direct-address style, not whether the correction given is right or whether the tone is appropriate.
proposals.rationale: R40 ('You did it correctly. You just made a little arithmetic mistake...') and R54 ('...is not quite right. You should have instead...') are written as personal corrections to the asker, unlike R06 or R31 which read as reference material for any future reader; this audience orientation is a fingerprint of the answerer's purpose, though personalized answers may also be more responsive and hence genuinely better.
proposals.upstream_parent: answerer's relationship to the reader (writing for the asker vs. for future searchers)

proposals.name: Terse hint-led opening
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the answer opens with a bare imperative label such as 'Hint:' or 'HINT:' followed by minimal restatement of the problem, versus a fuller worked exposition that restates context before proceeding. Score only the extent of this terse-hint-opening convention, not whether the hint given is sufficient or correct.
proposals.rationale: R17 ('Hint:\n\nI suppose that your mistake is...') and R33 ('HINT: Work up to it in steps...') open with the bare-hint convention typical of frequent site regulars, unlike R06 or R48 which build up more discursively; this register is a standing signal that could also correlate with genuinely efficient, correct answers from experienced posters.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice/standing in the format (a practiced regular's terse, declarative register)

proposals.name: Post-hoc edit/revision marker
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the text contains explicit revision markers such as 'EDIT:', 'Edit:', 'P.S.', or language flagging that material was added or corrected after the original post (e.g. 'I have three suggestions', 'this is broken'). Score only the extent of these revision markers, not whether the edit made the answer better or worse.
proposals.rationale: R35 ('EDIT: I have three suggestions...') and R45 ('edit: And well, this is broken.') both carry visible post-hoc revision markers absent from single-pass answers like R23 or R32; an editing history is an upstream production-process trace that could also indicate a genuinely more carefully corrected final answer.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing / editing behavior after initial posting

proposals.name: Cross-reference to other answers/users in thread
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the answer explicitly references, builds on, or presupposes other answers, comments, or named users on the same question -- e.g. 'to expand on X's answer', 'as mentioned before', 'I've just repeated Y's comment'. Score only the extent of this cross-referencing language, not whether the reference is accurate or whether building on it adds value.
proposals.rationale: R22 ('To expand on Stephen's answer:') and R57 ('I see I've just repeated Daniel Schepler's comment here.') both presuppose a populated answer thread, unlike R01 or R25 which engage the raw question from scratch; this is exactly the container-position fingerprint the mode-3 instructions call for, though a later, synthesizing answer could also be genuinely more complete.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream (arriving after other answers already exist)

proposals.name: Self-deprecating/apologetic hedge
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the answer contains self-deprecating or apologetic language about its own merit, completeness, or elegance -- e.g. 'this is broken', 'I'm not sure you can do better', 'I wouldn't say it is an elegant demonstration'. Score only the extent of such hedging language, not whether the hedge is actually warranted by the math.
proposals.rationale: R45 ('And well, this is broken.') and R46 ('I wouldn't say it is "elegant" demonstration; but I can't see how it could be more.') both editorialize about their own shortcomings in ways orthogonal to whether the underlying content is correct, unlike confidently flat answers like R18 or R32; this hedging register is treated as a pure style tell.
proposals.upstream_parent: answerer's confidence/self-assessed standing

proposals.name: Named external authority citation
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the answer invokes a named external authority beyond what is strictly required to state the result -- a named theorem (e.g. 'Clairaut's theorem'), a named colleague, an institution, or a course -- as opposed to deriving everything from bare notation and definitions alone. Score only the extent of such named-authority invocation, not whether the citation is correct, relevant, or necessary.
proposals.rationale: R25 opens by naming 'Clairaut's theorem' before giving a direct proof, and R35 name-drops 'My colleague, Chris Cooper... at Macquarie University'; neither citation is required by the math itself, unlike the bare-notation proofs in R03 or R32, so this is a fingerprint of the answerer's habits of reference that could also correlate with genuine subject mastery.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's scholarly practice/exposure to named literature and institutions

proposals.name: Narrative/pedagogical intuition framing
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the answer explicitly frames itself as building intuition for a broad audience -- e.g. 'let me give you an intuitive interpretation', 'one immediate way to wrap your mind around this' -- versus proceeding directly with compressed formal derivation and no meta-commentary about how to think about the problem. Score only the extent of this narrative-framing language, not whether the intuition offered is actually sound or helpful.
proposals.rationale: R06 ('Let me give you an intuitive... interpretation of entropy... let me justify it') and R19 ('One immediate... way to wrap your mind around this is...') both explicitly narrate their own pedagogical approach at length, unlike compressed answers like R07 or R23; this narrative framing is a stylistic habit that could also track genuinely more didactically effective writing.
proposals.upstream_parent: answerer's teaching orientation / motivation to write for future searchers rather than just the asker

proposals.name: Routine-computation vs conceptual question phrasing
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the QUESTION as shown (not the answer) is phrased as a closed-form routine computational task with a specific numeric or symbolic target -- e.g. 'Find the 8th derivative...', 'calculation of...' -- as opposed to an open conceptual, 'why', or 'explain' style question. Score only the extent of this routine-computation phrasing in the question text, not whether the question is well-posed or the answer addresses it successfully.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('Find the 8th derivative of the function... using sequences') and R20 ('calculation of $\int...$') pose narrowly-targeted computational tasks, while R06 ('Intuitive explanation of entropy') and R34 pose open conceptual questions; question genre can shape both the volunteer pool and the eventual crowd size independent of within-question preference, though harder conceptual questions may also make genuine quality easier to discriminate.
proposals.upstream_parent: kind of question the answer is attached to (routine homework computation vs. conceptual crowd-drawing question)

proposals.name: Pinpoints the asker's exact erroneous line and repairs it
proposals.instruction: Score how precisely the answer locates the specific step in the asker's own attempt that went wrong and supplies the corrected version of that step. 10 = the answer quotes or restates the asker's own expression, identifies the exact operation (a sign, a term, a differentiation step, a quantifier) that is wrong, and writes the fixed line; the asker could apply the fix without re-deriving anything. 5 = says the attempt contains an error and gestures at the region ('your mistake is probably in the integral') without exhibiting the corrected line. 0 = the answer presents an independent solution or general theory and never touches the asker's own work, or there is no indication the answer read the attempt at all.
proposals.rationale: The disagreement slice is full of surgical error-repairs the scorecard ranks near the bottom: R12 (dense .988 / card .148) does nothing but locate one sign slip and rewrite the single offending line; R28 (dense .943 / card .236) marks the wrong sign in red and says 'the error starts at the very beginning'; R30 and R35 both correct one specific mis-differentiation or mis-quantification. A criterion bank scoring mathematical content in the abstract sees these as thin, because most of the content lives in the asker's post, not the answer. Contrast R20 (dense .231 / card .825), which only guesses at where the mistake might be ('I suppose that your mistake is...') and then re-does the algebra generically.

proposals.name: Opens with a direct verdict on the question actually asked
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer's first move is an explicit verdict on the asker's literal question (yes / no / your work is correct / this is impossible) rather than an unannounced launch into derivation. 10 = the opening clause is an unambiguous verdict addressed to the asker's framing, and everything after it is support for that verdict. 5 = the verdict is present but buried after a paragraph of setup, or is only inferable from the derivation. 0 = the answer never states a verdict; the reader must reconstruct the answer to the yes/no question from the mathematics presented.
proposals.rationale: Several very short items that the scorecard scores near the floor lead with the verdict: R15 (dense .785 / card .154) is literally 'Yes. Since Z is free, the sequence splits'; R56 (dense .781 / card .145) opens 'That looks fine to me'; R59 (dense .872 / card .178) opens 'Your DFA looks good to me'; R23 (dense .732 / card .020) answers 'yes' to the asked question and only then adds the caveat. A content-bank scorecard has almost nothing to reward in a five-word verdict, but a reader who asked a yes/no question is served entirely by it. The inverse case is R41 (dense .289 / card .840): a correct, self-contained mod-3 argument that never says whether the asker's search was doomed or where their approach broke.

proposals.name: Machinery is proportionate to the crux, not to the topic
proposals.instruction: Judge the ratio between the apparatus deployed and the actual conceptual obstacle in the question. 10 = the answer isolates the one identity, factorization, or observation on which the question turns and stops there, so the reader sees the crux naked. 5 = the crux is reached but padded with routine steps the asker plainly already knows. 0 = a heavy, general, multi-stage apparatus is unrolled for an obstacle that a single line would clear, so the crux is buried in machinery. Judge proportionality against the difficulty visible in the question, not against absolute length.
proposals.rationale: R06 (dense .844 / card .202) answers a rational-expression puzzle with the single line a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b) plus the a+b != 0 caveat; R14 (dense .827 / card .216) collapses an absolute-value case analysis to a symmetry remark. Both are dense-high and card-low. Pulling the other way, R58 (dense .232 / card .956) writes out a full 3x3 cofactor matrix to reach a 2x2 determinant identity, and R31 (dense .265 / card .814) formally names f and g and composes them to differentiate an exponential. The scorecard evidently reads volume of correct apparatus as quality; the dense model appears to read apparatus-per-crux the other way.

proposals.name: Hint hands back a specific next action rather than a formula
proposals.instruction: For answers that deliberately withhold the full solution, score whether the withholding is constructive. 10 = the answer stages the remaining work as named steps or a pointed question the asker can act on immediately ('show X; then show Y; then apply both twice'; 'which terms survive at x=0?'), so the asker knows exactly what to do next. 5 = a relevant fact or substitution is offered but the asker must guess how it connects to their problem. 0 = a bare formula, expression, or assertion is dropped with the label 'hint' and no route from it to the goal. Answers that give the complete solution are scored on whether an equivalent next-step structure is present in the exposition; a complete, well-staged solution can score high.
proposals.rationale: R19 (dense .952 / card .344) is nothing but a three-rung ladder ending in 'apply (1) and (2) twice'; R43 (dense .845 / card .165) shows the expansion and then asks the asker which terms matter at x=0. Both are card-low. Compare R51 (dense .076 / card .631), a 'hint' that is a closed-form infinite sum with no indication of how to evaluate it, and R52's card score (.113) versus its dense .850 despite being a chain of substitutions. The scorecard appears to penalize incompleteness uniformly; the dense model seems to distinguish scaffolding from abandonment.

proposals.name: Stands on the question versus leans on other answers
proposals.instruction: Score how self-standing the answer is with respect to the rest of the thread, using only textual cues. 10 = the answer is framed entirely against the question and would read identically as the only answer present. 5 = it makes a passing reference to another post but its own contribution is complete without it. 0 = the answer is constituted as commentary on, correction of, or expansion of another answer ('to expand on X's answer', 'as was pointed out in another answer', 'as mentioned before', 'it's not clear why X's step is true'), so its content cannot be understood without the other post.
proposals.rationale: R57 (dense .194 / card .790) opens 'To expand on Stephen's answer'; R44 (dense .274 / card .826) opens 'As was pointed out in another answer'; R17 (dense .365-neighborhood, .095 / card .932) opens 'As mentioned before' and 'As in my post'; R02 (dense .080 / card .691) is a critique of Ove Ahlman's answer. All four are dense-low and card-high. A criterion bank judging the mathematics in isolation cannot see that the post is a satellite; a reader picking among answers to the same question can. Note the boundary case R45 (dense .648 / card .022), which credits @ErickWong for one residual case but is otherwise self-standing, so the low end must be reserved for structural dependence, not politeness.

proposals.name: Diagnoses the conceptual confusion, not just the symptom
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer identifies and treats the misunderstanding that produced the question, as opposed to only executing the requested manipulation. 10 = the answer explicitly names the conflation or false belief driving the question ('you are confusing the span of a subset with a spanning set', 'the surprising thing is that not all infinite sets have the same cardinality') and reorganizes the reader's picture around the correction. 5 = the answer supplies a correct result plus some interpretation, without locating a misconception. 0 = a purely mechanical response to the surface request.
proposals.rationale: R55 (dense .994 / card .026) spends its whole length separating two concepts the asker has conflated and never computes anything; R13 (dense .681 / card .056) treats the asker's discomfort with a proper subset being equipotent to its superset as the real question; R23 (dense .732 / card .020) explains why re-centering a series changes the region of convergence; R32 (dense .770 / card .151) explains why THM can be a proper subset of an inductive set. These have the four lowest card percentiles in the slice while sitting well above the dense median, which suggests the bank has little purchase on misconception-repair as such.

proposals.name: Validates what is already right before correcting
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer explicitly certifies the correct portion of the asker's work in addition to fixing the wrong portion. 10 = the answer states clearly which parts are right ('everything else you wrote is correct', 'your derivative for RHS is correct', 'that looks fine to me'), so the asker learns the scope of the error as well as the error. 5 = the correction implies but does not state that the rest stands. 0 = the answer either only corrects, leaving the asker unsure how far the damage extends, or does not engage with the asker's work.
proposals.rationale: R12 (dense .988 / card .148) closes with 'keep doing what you're doing because other than that mistake everything else you wrote is correct'; R30 (dense .867 / card .264) says the RHS derivative is correct but the notation is bad; R56 and R59 both open by certifying the asker's argument and then add the missing piece; R28 (dense .943 / card .236) says 'you are correct except one sign'. Scope-of-error information is worth a great deal to the asker and is invisible to any criterion that scores the answer's own mathematics.

proposals.name: Names a canonical object as a load-bearing shortcut, not as trivia
proposals.instruction: When the answer invokes a named theorem or named object, score whether the name does work. 10 = naming it immediately settles or reorganizes the question (invoking the theorem is the answer, or the isomorphism to a known classified object reduces the problem to lookup). 5 = the name is correct and relevant but the answer would be unchanged without it. 0 = the name is decorative -- supplied as interesting background alongside a derivation that never uses it -- or no naming occurs where one would obviously help.
proposals.rationale: R11 (dense .941 / card .260) opens by observing the hypotheses violate Clairaut's theorem, which settles the question outright; R21 (dense .764 / card .150) is one line, G/Z(G) = Inn(G), which converts the exercise into a lookup; R42 (dense .820 / card .212) reduces the problem to the known subgroup lattice of D_6. Against these, R40 (dense .379 / card .924) names the director circle 'for the sake of interest' and then grinds through Vieta anyway, and R10 (dense .116 / card .739) names the order-statistics family as an aside. Same surface feature -- a correct technical name -- pulling opposite ways, which is exactly the kind of distinction a flat criterion would blur.

proposals.name: Sustained second-person address to this asker
proposals.instruction: Score how consistently the answer is written to the person who asked, using the text alone. 10 = second-person address runs through the answer, the asker's own notation and framing are adopted, and the answer checks comprehension or anticipates the asker's next confusion. 5 = occasional 'you' inside an otherwise impersonal exposition. 0 = fully impersonal exposition in the answer's own notation, indistinguishable from a textbook passage on the topic.
proposals.rationale: R04 (dense .945 / card .229) reads the asker's own stem-and-leaf rows back to them and ends 'Does that make sense?'; R55 says 'you seem to be greatly confused' and then 'let me dispel that confusion'; R38 (dense .784 / card .177) walks the asker through their own expression and ends 'hopefully this shows...'. Opposite pole: R50 (dense .282 / card .998, the highest card score in the slice) is a polished impersonal essay on entropy addressed to no one in particular, and R18 (dense .095 / card .932) is a generic grid explanation. Register is exactly the kind of property an explicit-criterion bank tends to omit as non-mathematical.

proposals.name: Self-standing polish combined with untailored generality
proposals.instruction: Score the composite: high textual polish and completeness TOGETHER WITH absence of any purchase on this particular asker's situation. 10 = long, well-formatted, self-contained, and entirely generic -- it answers the topic rather than the post, and could be moved to any similar question unchanged. 0 = the answer is inseparable from this post: it uses the asker's variables, their attempt, their stated sticking point. Intermediate scores for answers that are tailored in places and generic elsewhere. This criterion deliberately scores high for polished generality; it measures a property, not a merit.
proposals.rationale: The card-high tail of the slice is dominated by this shape: R50 (card .998), R58 (card .956), R48 (card .948), R46 (card .874), R37 (card 1.000) are all extended, well-organized, self-contained treatments with no visible contact with the asker's own attempt, and all sit at dense .150-.417. Because the scorecard reads each answer in isolation, polish and completeness are the only things it can see, and this shape maximizes them. Scoring the property explicitly lets the disagreement be modeled rather than absorbed.

proposals.name: Reframing that dissolves the computation
proposals.instruction: Score whether the answer replaces the expected grind with a change of representation that makes the result nearly immediate. 10 = a substitution, symmetry, rewriting rule, or reformulation is introduced that visibly collapses the problem, and the answer makes clear why the reframing is the right move. 5 = a standard technique is applied competently along the expected route. 0 = the answer marches through the brute-force route the asker was already on, or introduces a reframing without indicating why it helps.
proposals.rationale: R22 (dense .977 / card .175) rewrites e^{|x|} as e^{sgn(x)x} and gets the antiderivative in one line; R34 (dense .955 / card .274) notices every derivative of xe^x has the form (x+c_n)e^x and turns an eighth-derivative request into a one-step recursion; R39 (dense .883 / card .272) completes the square to make a digit-sum question tractable; R26 (dense .913 / card .275) rewrites the n-th-root difference as a telescoped quotient to get the bound. All four are card-low. The bank appears to score correctness and completeness of the route taken rather than the leverage of the route chosen.

proposals.name: Hedged ownership of one's own claim
proposals.instruction: Score the answer's epistemic stance toward its own content. 10 = the answer commits: assertions are made flatly and any stated caveat is a precise mathematical condition rather than personal uncertainty. 0 = the answer is framed as a guess or a work in progress ('I think I have the answer', 'I think the statement is false', 'I'm not sure you can do better', 'I would do something like that', requests for someone else to verify or clean it up). Score the framing, not whether the mathematics is right, which you are not asked to adjudicate.
proposals.rationale: The hedged items cluster hard in the card-high half: R17 (dense .095 / card .932) 'I think I have the answer using generating functions'; R29 (dense .209 / card .787) 'I think the statement is false'; R05 (dense .047 / card .927) 'I think you could divide it into some easier parts'; R53 (dense .142 / card .686) 'I'm not sure you can do better'; R40 closes by asking someone to fix its TeX; R16 (dense .131 / card .989) closes with 'I am not 100% sure that you weren't aware of all that already'. Meanwhile the committed one-liners R15 and R21 sit dense-high and card-low. Hedging is a surface feature a text-blind content bank will not charge for.

proposals.name: Refutation carried through to a repair
proposals.instruction: For answers that show a claim in the question is false, score whether they carry on past the refutation. 10 = the counterexample is exhibited AND the answer supplies what the asker actually needs next: the corrected statement, the extra hypothesis that rescues it, or the reason the claim fails structurally. 5 = a fully verified counterexample with no repair. 0 = a bare refuting assertion or an unverified example dropped with no working and no repair. Answers that make no refutation are not applicable; score them 5.
proposals.rationale: R25 (dense .052 / card .601) is two lines: 'Consider the following curve. F(t)=(t^(3/2),0,0)' with no verification and no repair; R07 (dense .242 / card .938) constructs a clean counterexample in l^2 and stops; R29 (dense .209 / card .787) argues via Fourier transform that the claim fails and stops; R47 (dense .190 / card .781) answers 'False' and then drifts into conditions without settling one. R44, on the same question as R29, does supply a sufficient condition and sits slightly higher on dense (.274) while still card-high, so repair alone does not explain the gap -- which is why the criterion separates the two components.

proposals.name: Execution without explanation of why the route works
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the answer is uninterpreted symbol-pushing. 10 = every nontrivial move is executed and none is motivated: substitutions appear without justification, results are stated without saying what makes the method appropriate. 0 = each nontrivial move is accompanied by the reason it is the right move, so the reader could reproduce the choice on a new problem. This criterion scores a property (execution-only-ness), not merit.
proposals.rationale: R08 (dense .211 / card .908) performs the u-substitution flawlessly and says nothing about why x^4+5 is the substitution to make; R31 (dense .265 / card .814) applies the chain rule with full formal notation and no word about the idea; R09 (dense .068 / card .806) asserts 'you mixed them up' and shows one column of the composition; R60 (dense .150 / card .729) computes T on four basis elements and stops. All four are correct, complete, and card-high. A criterion bank built around correctness and completeness will rate flawless execution highly by construction, and a reader choosing among answers to the same question may not.

proposals.name: Exposition that leaves the reader the last step, cleanly
proposals.instruction: Score the composite: the answer resolves the conceptual content fully AND deliberately leaves a clearly-delimited routine remainder to the reader, naming what that remainder is. 10 = every idea is supplied, the remaining work is explicitly identified as mechanical ('I leave it to you to simplify this expression', 'now you have to figure out when it becomes periodic'), and the reader knows the answer is complete in the ways that matter. 5 = complete through to the final expression with nothing left. 0 = the answer stops short of resolving the conceptual content, leaving a genuine gap rather than a routine one, without saying so.
proposals.rationale: The cleanest pair in the slice is R33 and R27, two answers to the identical ball-counting question. R33 (dense .968 / card .251) derives the sum and then writes 'I leave it you to simplify this expression'; R27 (dense .288 / card .867) carries the same sum all the way to (n+2)2^{n-1} with a footnote proving an auxiliary identity. The scorecard puts the fully-carried-out one nearly six deciles higher and the dense model reverses it, which says the extra algebra is not what a reader wanted. R36 (dense .962 / card .250) shows the same shape: three long-division steps, then 'now you have to figure out when it becomes periodic'.

proposals.name: Presupposition that other answers already exist
proposals.instruction: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the wording presupposes that other answers, or prior discussion of this same question, already exist at the moment of writing. Count constructions such as: explicit reference to another answer or to what was 'pointed out', 'mentioned', or 'said' before; offers of an alternative, shorter, or supplementary route ('a bit shorter', 'to expand on', 'for the sake of interest', 'another way'); deferral of a sub-case to someone else's treatment; corrections or qualifications aimed at a prior posted argument rather than at the question itself. 0 = the text engages the raw question completely from scratch, with no linguistic sign that anything has yet been said; 5 = one passing gesture toward prior material; 10 = the answer is framed throughout as an addition, correction, or alternative to material already present. You MUST NOT judge whether referring to prior answers is gracious, redundant, helpful, or correct, and you must not judge answer quality in any way. Score only how much of this presupposition is textually present.
