proposals.rationale: This is a pure positional fingerprint, not a property of the mathematics. R01 opens 'As was pointed out in another answer'; R33 opens 'To expand on Stephen's answer'; R19 argues against a claim 'in Ove Ahlman's answer'; R21 defers a case with 'This case is already nicely considered in the answer from @ErickWong'; R60 opens 'A bit shorter:'. Contrast R18, which addresses the SAME question as R01 but from scratch ('I think the statement is false'), and R34, which addresses the same question as R10 with no reference to it. Arrival order is invisible to a text model except through this trace, so it is a nuisance route; tagged mixed because a late answerer who has read the earlier ones can genuinely write a better-targeted answer.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream (how many answers had already been posted when this one was written)

proposals.name: Vintage of notation and markup conventions
proposals.instruction: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the mathematical notation and markup look like an older vintage of this site's conventions rather than current practice. Traces to count: mathematics typed as plain ASCII with no math delimiters at all (things like t^(3/2), >=, x^2 written bare in prose); raw Unicode operator and arrow glyphs pasted inline where a markup macro would now be used; abbreviated blackboard-bold and older macro spellings rather than their long modern forms; older combinatorial and number-theoretic shorthands (pre-superscript binomial forms, 'hcf' rather than 'gcd', subfactorial written with a leading bang); a single undifferentiated display block where a modern post would use an aligned multi-line environment; prose typographic habits such as double-dot ellipses, spaces before punctuation, or emoticons. 0 = uniformly current, environment-rich markup; 10 = heavily dated or markup-free throughout. You MUST NOT judge whether the notation is clear, correct, or good; score only how much dated-convention texture is present.
proposals.rationale: Era leaves a notational stamp but is shared by every answer on the same thread, so it cannot causally move a WITHIN-question comparison against sibling answers, while it can still shift a pool-wide model score. R24 is bare ASCII ('F(t)=(t^(3/2),0,0) where t>=0'); R12 pastes raw Unicode implication and inequality glyphs inline and writes '2nd note:'; R16 uses the old pre-superscript combination shorthand and the leading-bang subfactorial; R33 writes 'hcf(n,i)'; R23 uses the abbreviated blackboard-bold macro; R55 uses double-dot ellipses as prose punctuation. Purely a dating fingerprint, hence not mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: the era of the site the post comes from (post vintage)

proposals.name: Fluency with display-math environments and equation machinery
proposals.instruction: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the author operates the site's mathematical typesetting machinery like a habitual user. Traces to count: multi-line aligned environments with alignment markers; matrix and determinant environments; hand-numbered or tagged equations that are later referred to by their number; colour macros or other emphasis macros inside mathematics; operator-name macros rather than italic prose; sectioning, block quoting, or set-off statement banners; deliberate spacing macros. Score DOWN for the opposite texture: mathematics dropped inline as one long undelimited run, delimiters used inconsistently, or an explicit request for help fixing the typesetting. 0 = no machinery at all beyond plain inline math; 10 = dense, confident, multi-device typesetting throughout. You MUST NOT judge whether the typesetting is attractive, readable, or appropriate to the content, and you must not judge answer quality. Score only how much machinery is exercised.
proposals.rationale: Markup fluency is a habit acquired by posting a lot here, not a property of the argument. R04 runs matrix and determinant environments and numbers its equations with tags it then cites back ('(0)', '(*)', '(1)', '(2)', '(3)'); R21 uses aligned environments, colour macros and operator-name macros with banner-style case headers; R22 and R35 use aligned multi-line derivations. At the other pole R32 ends with '(can somebody please fix up my TeX so the chunk equations is centred and aligned?)' and R24 uses no markup at all. Tagged mixed because a practised regular plausibly also writes genuinely better answers.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's accumulated practice and standing in this format (a site regular versus an occasional poster)

proposals.name: Orthographic slips and informal typing hygiene
proposals.instruction: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT of surface language-production slips: chat-style abbreviations of ordinary words (single-letter 'U' for 'you', 'cause' for 'because'), missing spaces after sentence-final or list punctuation, spaces placed before commas, misspellings of ordinary or technical English words, non-standard comparative or plural forms, dropped function words that make a phrase ungrammatical, unmatched or improvised quotation marks around ordinary terms, and run-on sentences with commas doing the work of periods. 0 = clean, conventionally edited English; 10 = slips of these kinds in most sentences. Do NOT count mathematical errors, and do NOT count deliberate informality that is otherwise correctly written. You MUST NOT judge whether the writing is good, professional, or easy to read; score only the density of these surface slips.
proposals.rationale: A typing-hygiene trace that a text model can read off directly while it says nothing about within-question crowd preference on its own. R10 writes 'U have', 'U want', 'Simplier', 'chosing'; R17 writes 'You mixed them up.If you look at' and ',firstly at'; R12 writes 'switchs' and long comma-spliced sentences; R03 writes 'independant'; R34 writes 'I leave it you to simplify'. Tagged mixed because hurried or non-native composition may co-occur with genuinely less careful mathematics.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's language background and how much composition care the post received

proposals.name: Bulk: overall length and count of display blocks
proposals.instruction: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT of sheer textual bulk, combining three countable things in roughly equal weight: total word count of the prose, the number of separate set-off displayed-mathematics blocks, and the number of paragraph or list-item breaks. Calibrate so that 0 = a single sentence or a single line of mathematics with essentially no prose; 3 = one short paragraph plus one display; 6 = several paragraphs with three to five displays; 10 = many screens of prose interleaved with numerous displays, tables, or enumerated case sections. You MUST NOT judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the answer is padded, or whether it is admirably concise. Score only the amount of material present.
proposals.rationale: The classic verbosity proxy, declared a nuisance so it can never enter the criterion bank. It varies enormously across the slice and even within a single thread: R10 and R34 answer the SAME question, and R10 runs many paragraphs with six displays while R34 is three short paragraphs with one; R04, R20, R21, R12 and R15 are multi-screen, whereas R27 is one sentence, R13 two lines, R05 one sentence, R24 two lines and R40 one sentence. Because the conjectured parent is surface-only, the channel is not mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Visible revision trace and appended afterthoughts
proposals.instruction: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text visibly shows that it was revised or extended after first being written. Traces to count: an explicit edit marker in any casing, followed by added material; postscript markers; numbered follow-up notes appended after the argument has concluded; a coda that comments on the answer itself or on how it came to be extended; material that reads as bolted on to satisfy a follow-up rather than as part of the original plan; a trailing fragment that starts a new topic and stops. 0 = a single continuously composed piece with no revision markers; 10 = multiple clearly demarcated later additions. You MUST NOT judge whether the revisions improved the answer or whether editing is a virtue; score only how much revision trace is visible.
proposals.rationale: Editing happens off-page, in comments and re-visits, and is only knowable through these markers. R06 has 'EDIT: I have three suggestions for treating the intersection'; R26 has 'Edit: I wouldn't worry about it too much'; R58 ends 'edit: And well, this is broken.'; R54 ends on a dangling 'EDIT.' fragment; R36 carries a postscript recounting that it had earlier computed only one case and was extended for a second user; R47 and R12 append postscript and '2nd note:' codas. Tagged mixed because revision prompted by reader feedback plausibly also makes the answer genuinely better.
proposals.upstream_parent: post-hoc editing driven by comment-thread interaction after posting

proposals.name: Diagnosing the asker's posted attempt versus standalone exposition
proposals.instruction: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the answer is addressed to one particular person's already-posted work rather than written as a self-contained exposition for a general reader. Traces to count: second-person verdicts on that person's attempt ('you did it correctly', 'that looks fine to me', 'you are correct except', 'you mixed them up', 'you seem to be confused'); quotation of the asker's own lines or symbols back at them; localisation of a specific slip to a specific step or sign; instructions phrased as what 'you' should do next with 'your' expression; conversational check-ins directed at that person. Score LOW when the text never presumes any prior attempt and reads as an exposition a stranger could land on cold. 0 = fully standalone exposition; 10 = line-by-line correction of one person's posted work throughout. You MUST NOT judge whether personal, corrective engagement is helpful or whether standalone exposition is better; score only which mode of address is present and how strongly.
proposals.rationale: This distinguishes two writing stances that are driven by the thread situation, not by mathematical merit. R57 opens 'You did it correctly. You just made a little arithmetic mistake near the end'; R35 opens 'You are correct except one sign'; R41 opens 'That looks fine to me'; R06 opens 'Your DFA looks good to me'; R09, R44 and R53 all diagnose the asker's own construction. At the other pole R15 and R20 are self-contained expositions addressed to no one in particular, and R50 explains a general trick. Tagged mixed because a well-aimed diagnosis of the asker's specific error can be genuinely what the thread needed.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's relationship to the reader (writing for the asker versus for future searchers), which is itself set by whether the question posted a visible attempt

proposals.name: Social embedding: named people, institutions, cross-links
proposals.instruction: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text is socially embedded in a named community rather than anonymous. Traces to count: named individuals, whether real names, handles, or site usernames; at-mentions; references to a named institution, course, colleague, or set of local notes; pointers to other threads or questions on the site, quoted by title or as a see-also; references to material the author says they posted elsewhere or previously; attributions of a step or a case to a specific other person. 0 = no person, institution, or off-page pointer named anywhere; 10 = several such references woven through the text. You MUST NOT judge whether the references are appropriate, well-chosen, or self-promotional, and you must not judge answer quality. Score only how much naming and pointing is present.
proposals.rationale: Knowing who else is in the thread and what else the site contains is a function of tenure, not of the mathematics. R06 names 'My colleague, Chris Cooper' and 'Macquarie University'; R36 names 'user142198' and another user 'Exam in 5 days'; R21 attributes a case to '@ErickWong'; R19 cites 'Ove Ahlman's answer'; R33 cites 'Stephen's answer'; R23 points to another thread by title ('See for example How many subgroups of order n does D_n have?'). Tagged mixed because a long-tenured author plausibly also writes genuinely better answers.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's tenure, standing, and social network on the site (a long-time regular who knows the other regulars and the back catalogue)

proposals.name: Hint-mode withholding versus delivered completion
proposals.instruction: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the answer deliberately stops short and hands the remaining work back to the reader. Traces to count: an explicit hint label opening the post, in any casing; a numbered programme of things the reader is told to 'show' or 'prove' themselves; explicit statements that the remainder is left to the reader or that the reader should now simplify, finish, or figure out what happens next; a closing question put back to the reader; a final line that names the next step without taking it. Score LOW when the argument is carried all the way to a stated conclusion or final value. 0 = complete worked argument ending in its conclusion; 10 = nothing but a pointer or opening move with the work explicitly delegated. You MUST NOT judge whether hinting is pedagogically right or whether a full solution is better; score only how much of the work is withheld.
proposals.rationale: Hint-mode is a house style acquired from the venue, and it is orthogonal to whether the mathematics behind it is sound. R29 opens 'HINT: Work up to it in steps:' and lists three things for the reader to show; R07, R39, R42, R43 and R59 all open with a hint label; R23 opens 'Hint:' and then points elsewhere; R34 closes 'I leave it you to simplify this expression'; R22 closes 'Now you have to figure out when it becomes periodic'; R26 closes 'Does that make sense?'. Contrast R31 and R14, which carry a full argument to its contradiction. Tagged mixed because a practised answerer's judgement about how much to withhold may itself track what the thread wanted.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's habitual pedagogical practice in this format and the homework-answering norms they were socialised into

proposals.name: Flat declarative assertion versus epistemic hedging
proposals.instruction: Read only the answer text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT of flat, unhedged declarative assertion, scoring the hedged pole low. Score HIGH for: verdicts delivered as bare single words or single sentences before any argument; assertions with no epistemic qualifier; 'it is clear', 'it is easy to check', 'of course', 'obviously', 'we are done'. Score LOW for: first-person uncertainty ('I think', 'I'm not sure', 'I suppose', 'I believe', 'maybe'), self-deprecation about the author's own contribution, scare-quoted disclaimers that the treatment is only intuitive or non-rigorous, apologies, expressions of doubt about whether the reader already knew this, and closing pleasantries that solicit approval. 0 = pervasively hedged and tentative; 10 = flatly declarative throughout. You MUST NOT judge whether the confidence is warranted, whether the claims are correct, or whether hedging is honest; score only the register.
proposals.rationale: Register, not content: the same mathematical claim can be delivered either way. Flat pole: R27 is 'Yes. Since Z is free, the sequence splits and you get what you want.'; R45 opens with the bare verdict 'False' then 'Proof:'; R13 asserts a factorisation and a condition with no qualifier; R14 says 'It is easy to check that'; R21 repeatedly closes cases with 'and we are done'. Hedged pole: R18 opens 'I think the statement is false'; R28 opens 'I think I have the answer using generating functions'; R40 says 'I'm not sure you can do better'; R12 closes 'I am not 100% sure that you weren't aware of all that already'; R46 labels itself 'An "engineering" explanation'; R54 closes 'Hope this helps!'. Tagged mixed because the underlying standing plausibly also produces genuinely better answers.
proposals.upstream_parent: the answerer's standing and experience in the format (a confident regular's willingness to be terse and flatly declarative versus a newer poster's hedging)

proposals.name: Misconception diagnosis and repair
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer identifies the exact conceptual mistake, explains why it is wrong, and supplies the corrected reasoning; score 0 when it merely states a result or repeats an unexplained correction.
proposals.rationale: R02 distinguishes spanning sets from spans and repairs the underlying confusion; R47 explains the quantifier mistake before continuing the subgroup proof.

proposals.name: Concrete contradiction construction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a false claim is refuted by a concrete, valid counterexample or contradiction whose decisive property is explicitly verified; score 0 when falsity is asserted without a usable demonstration.
proposals.rationale: R17 uses Fourier behavior near zero to construct an obstruction; R23 gives an explicit function and explains why all antiderivatives fail to be square-integrable.

proposals.name: Assumption and domain control
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer explicitly tracks domains, excluded values, branches, convergence conditions, or theorem hypotheses throughout; score 0 when such conditions are ignored or silently violated.
proposals.rationale: R01 discusses the interval of convergence after recentering; R49 tracks logarithm branches and integer periodicity when solving a complex equation.

proposals.name: Stepwise mechanism over result assertion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer exposes a reproducible sequence of transformations that makes the result follow; score 0 when it gives only a final answer, verdict, or opaque hint.
proposals.rationale: R20 transforms the polynomial into a useful completed-square form; R39 systematically reduces infinitely many integer cases to residue classes and then handles them.

proposals.name: Useful abstraction with concrete payoff
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an abstract theorem, structure, or representation is introduced and immediately connected to the specific problem; score 0 when abstraction is ornamental or disconnected from the requested conclusion.
proposals.rationale: R13 uses holomorphic logarithms and the identity theorem to organize the branch construction; R18 interprets cycle powers as modular translations to make enumeration immediate.

proposals.name: Intuition tied to formal meaning
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an accessible analogy or geometric interpretation is explicitly linked to the relevant definition or formula; score 0 when the analogy is vague, misleading, or never connected back to mathematics.
proposals.rationale: R16 connects entropy to expected code length and then states the mathematical bound; R15 explains sampling density through grid counts and the relation N=k^p.

proposals.name: Boundary-case and exceptional-case coverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer identifies and handles the cases that could invalidate the main argument, including endpoints, parity, zero denominators, or exceptional parameters; score 0 when it treats only a generic case.
proposals.rationale: R51 separates odd and even numbers of bulbs and tracks reachable parity; R04 carries endpoint inequalities through nested functions and inverse cotangent.

proposals.name: Error containment and correction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer notices an erroneous intermediate claim, clearly marks its scope, and replaces it with a valid argument; score 0 when an error remains unrecognized or contaminates the conclusion.
proposals.rationale: R33 explicitly acknowledges that its sign-function antiderivative is broken; R40 pinpoints the first sign error and reconstructs the factorization afterward.

proposals.name: Independent verification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer checks its derivation by a second method, substitution, structural identity, or direct verification; score 0 when no check is provided and the main calculation is difficult to audit.
proposals.rationale: R08 confirms the derivative recurrence with a Taylor expansion; R44 recommends substituting the parameterized solution back into both equations.

proposals.name: Appropriate completeness for the question
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer supplies enough argument to establish the requested claim without making the reader fill in essential steps; score 0 when it is either an unsupported assertion or an unrelated overexpansion.
proposals.rationale: R31 fully applies the multivariable chain rule to the requested partial derivative; R52 compresses a relative-homology conclusion into a theorem invocation without showing the resulting decomposition.

proposals.name: Pedagogical alignment with the asker
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the response directly addresses the asker’s apparent sticking point using their notation or partial work and adjusts the explanation accordingly; score 0 when it ignores that context.
proposals.rationale: R14 computes each basis image after the asker struggled with those specific evaluations; R09 corrects the asker’s logarithmic derivative while preserving the valid right-hand differentiation.

proposals.name: Reusable generalization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer extracts a method, recurrence, template, or broader principle that applies beyond the displayed instance; score 0 when it solves only the immediate instance with no transferable insight.
proposals.rationale: R08 derives a recurrence for every derivative order; R24 generalizes the roots-of-unity divisibility trick from one polynomial to a wider exponent pattern.

proposals.name: Precise notation and object tracking
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every symbol, operation, object, and quantifier is used consistently and the reader can tell exactly what each expression denotes; score 0 when notation is ambiguous, malformed, or changes meaning.
proposals.rationale: R02 carefully separates a set, its ambient vector space, and its span; R35 clarifies permutation composition by tracking the image of a specific column through both maps.

proposals.name: Strategic hinting with actionable direction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a short response identifies the decisive idea and gives enough direction for the reader to execute it; score 0 when the hint is generic, inaccessible, or substitutes for an answer despite requiring substantial missing work.
proposals.rationale: R38 gives a sequence of monotonicity lemmas that directly reduces the Boolean-ordering proof; R60 points to inner automorphisms as a concrete route to an example.

proposals.name: Scope calibration and epistemic honesty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer accurately distinguishes what has been proved, what is merely sufficient, and what remains unresolved; score 0 when it overclaims, uses unjustified certainty, or presents a partial argument as complete.

proposals.name: Formalized conceptual analogy

proposals.name: Independent result verification

proposals.name: Misconception-targeted pedagogy

proposals.name: Explicit answer closure

proposals.name: Infinite-process justification

proposals.name: Economical sufficiency

proposals.name: Compressed hint style

proposals.name: Scaffolded exposition

proposals.name: Direct asker correction
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the answer directly addresses, corrects, reassures, or diagnoses the asker's work using second-person language; do not judge whether that interaction is good.
proposals.rationale: Second-person correction reveals an interactional context rather than a mathematical property. R11 and R20 reassure or correct the asker; R34 and R44 directly diagnose an error or sequencing issue.

proposals.name: Thread-position language
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the answer refers to other answers, prior remarks, additions, or alternative approaches in the surrounding thread; do not judge whether those references are good.

proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Era-marked conventions
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the extent of visibly period-marked notation, typography, markup, or vocabulary; do not judge whether the conventions are good or mathematically sound.

proposals.name: Revision trace markers
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the answer contains edit labels, postscripts, apologies, correction notes, or explicit repair language; do not judge whether the revisions improved the answer.
proposals.rationale: These markers expose how the post was produced and revised, independently of the underlying mathematics. R08, R16, R39, R46, and R55 visibly contain edits, postscripts, or repair commentary.

proposals.name: Site-native regular voice
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the extent of site-native shorthand, theorem-name references, terse declaratives, and familiar answer idioms; do not judge whether this voice is good.
proposals.rationale: A practiced format-specific voice can be a proxy for author standing while remaining distinct from mathematical content. R14 and R53 use hint-and-reference shorthand; R33 and R47 use practiced theorem-driven prompts.

proposals.name: Future-reader orientation
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the answer generalizes beyond the immediate problem through reusable methods, broader context, alternatives, or definitions; do not judge whether that orientation is good.

proposals.name: Question-genre imprint

proposals.name: Markup and display density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the visible density and regularity of display mathematics, aligned equations, matrices, custom macros, sectioning, and prose-to-formula balance; do not judge whether the presentation is clear or good.
proposals.rationale: Markup habits can proxy author practice and era while remaining separate from mathematical merit. R04 and R25 are display-heavy; R35, R43, and R49 show distinctive alignment, color, or product-format habits.

proposals.name: Decisive-error diagnosis and repair
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer pinpoints the exact invalid step and supplies the corrected reasoning; score 0 when it merely says something is wrong or gives an incorrect repair.
proposals.rationale: R17, R35, R40, and R50 all focus on locating a specific derivative, sign, substitution, or arithmetic error rather than redoing everything generically.

proposals.name: Domain-safe manipulation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer tracks denominator restrictions, branch choices, signs, endpoints, and validity conditions throughout; score 0 when it performs transformations that silently fail on part of the stated domain.

proposals.name: Self-contained completion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer reaches the requested conclusion with all essential definitions and steps included; score 0 when it is only a hint, approval, citation, or fragment that requires substantial reconstruction.
proposals.rationale: R10 and R11 provide partial computational guidance, while R16, R26, and R32 are especially dependent on the reader supplying missing work.

proposals.name: Learner-oriented conceptual bridge
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when abstract notation is connected to an accessible mental model and then tied back rigorously to the problem; score 0 when the answer is either unexplained jargon or an unsupported slogan.
proposals.rationale: R21, R30, R36, and R58 attempt to connect spans, cardinality, sampling density, or entropy to intuitive interpretations.

proposals.name: Generalizable method extraction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer clearly identifies a reusable strategy and demonstrates why it works; score 0 when it gives only an isolated calculation with no transferable method.
proposals.rationale: R18, R23, R39, and R47 expose recurring techniques involving recurrences, roots of unity, modular reduction, or cycle powers.

proposals.name: Concrete witness construction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an existence, nonexistence, or counterexample claim is supported by an explicit object whose required properties are checked; score 0 when the answer merely asserts or vaguely suggests such an object.
proposals.rationale: R26 offers only an example-producing hint, whereas R41, R51, and R56 illustrate how explicit curves, formal systems, or model constructions can settle the issue.

proposals.name: Proof-obligation closure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every nontrivial implication needed for the conclusion is justified and the final step is explicitly connected to the claim; score 0 when key transitions are hidden behind “clearly” or “therefore.”
proposals.rationale: R02, R13, R24, R42, and R60 contain chains where convergence, generating functions, ramification, or set inclusion require careful closure of intermediate obligations.

proposals.name: Symbolic consistency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when signs, exponents, indices, substitutions, and displayed equations remain mutually consistent; score 0 when an uncorrected local symbolic error undermines the calculation.
proposals.rationale: R05 contains an exponent inconsistency, while R35, R37, and R50 show how sign or arithmetic details materially affect otherwise plausible work.

proposals.name: Proportional method choice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the chosen technique is no more elaborate than necessary while still resolving the question rigorously; score 0 when the method is needlessly cumbersome, tangential, or mismatched to the task.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R10 show compact elementary routes, while R22 and R42 illustrate substantially heavier machinery for focused questions.

proposals.name: Explicit scope and counterconditions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer states the hypotheses under which a claim holds and identifies meaningful failure cases; score 0 when a broad statement is treated as unconditional.
proposals.rationale: R02, R04, R15, R38, R43, and R55 all depend on distinguishing universal claims from statements requiring integrability, positivity, convergence, or boundedness assumptions.

proposals.name: Structure-revealing transformation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a substitution, factorization, invariant, or change of representation makes the underlying structure evident and is explained; score 0 when algebraic transformations remain opaque or merely procedural.
proposals.rationale: R01 uses sheet and argument structure, R18 uses a derivative recurrence, R23 uses roots of unity, and R60 rewrites inequalities into tractable auxiliary functions.

proposals.name: Actionable pedagogical prompting
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer gives an ordered next step that the reader can execute, with enough information to continue independently; score 0 when it offers only vague encouragement or an unhelpful assertion.
proposals.rationale: R16, R27, R40, R46, and R59 use hints or corrections of varying actionability, ranging from concrete next operations to minimal prompts.

proposals.name: Calibrated partial validation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the answer accurately separates correct portions from incorrect ones and preserves the valid work; score 0 when it gives blanket approval, blanket rejection, or introduces a new error while correcting the reader.
proposals.rationale: R17, R35, R50, and R53 explicitly distinguish what is already valid from the precise part needing correction.

proposals.name: Notation and convention disambiguation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when ambiguous notation, operation order, object identity, or convention is explicitly interpreted before reasoning; score 0 when the answer relies on an unstated interpretation that could change the result.
proposals.rationale: R01, R09, R25, R28, and R29 involve branch notation, inverse functions, permutation order, or distinguishability conventions.

proposals.name: Independent verification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the conclusion is checked by a genuinely different derivation, invariant, limiting case, or direct substitution; score 0 when no check is offered or the purported check is circular.
proposals.rationale: R18 verifies the derivative sequence with a Taylor expansion, R19 gives an SVD-based confirmation, and R35, R37, and R42 use algebraic or arithmetic cross-checks.

proposals.name: Post-order add-on language
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the answer signals awareness of an existing answer sequence, such as adding, correcting, extending, or referring back to other answers; do not judge whether the answer is good.
proposals.rationale: Later placement may leave textual traces without representing mathematical merit. R01 says it repeats a comment, while R48 explicitly expands another answer; both exhibit position-sensitive language.

proposals.name: Era-marked notation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the answer displays notation, markup, vocabulary, or conventions characteristic of a particular StackExchange era; do not judge whether those conventions are good.
proposals.rationale: Historical posting norms can affect text style independently of mathematics. R40 uses colored legacy markup and extensive residue-like formatting, while R43 uses older-style equation tags and determinant presentation.

proposals.name: Regular-user register
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the prose resembles a practiced specialist answerer: terse declaratives, confident transitions, conventional notation, and compressed theorem-based exposition; do not judge mathematical quality.
proposals.rationale: Experienced participation can influence both reception-oriented style and genuine content, making it a mixed nuisance. R26 invokes SVD compactly, while R39 gives formal definitions in a highly practiced explanatory register.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format

proposals.name: Reader-orientation cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the answer addresses the immediate asker through correction, reassurance, hints, or conversational guidance versus addressing future readers through self-contained exposition; do not judge which orientation is better.
proposals.rationale: Audience orientation is a textual trace of an upstream social choice and can also affect substantive tailoring. R09 directly reassures and corrects the asker, whereas R16 frames a broad explanation for readers learning entropy.
proposals.upstream_parent: answerer's relationship to the reader

proposals.name: Revision provenance cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the answer exposes editing, correction, follow-up, or assistance history through labels such as 'Edit', 'P.S.', apologies, or explicit repairs; do not judge whether the repaired text is good.
proposals.rationale: Revision history can leave conspicuous linguistic residue unrelated to intrinsic mathematical merit, while editing may also alter content. R04 contains an explicit self-retraction, and R31 adds a postscript explaining later additions.

proposals.name: Social attribution signals
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the answer names, cites, credits, or points toward other people, answers, colleagues, or external notes; do not judge the authority or correctness of the references.
proposals.rationale: Network visibility can affect how text functions socially while also correlating with expertise, so this is mixed. R01 names Daniel Schepler's comment, and R60 mentions a colleague's course notes.

proposals.name: Question-genre markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the answer's vocabulary, notation, and explanatory level signal the attached question as routine instructional work, elementary troubleshooting, or specialist conceptual mathematics; do not judge the answer's quality.
proposals.rationale: Question genre creates different textual habitats and audience expectations without itself measuring answer merit. R03 is framed as a short calculus hint, while R38 uses specialist algebraic-number-theory terminology and extended exposition.

proposals.name: Boilerplate scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the presence and repetition of stock instructional phrases or templates such as 'Hint', 'Let', 'It is clear', 'You are correct', or 'For example'; do not judge whether the template is helpful.
proposals.rationale: Canned phrasing may be predictive as a stylistic fingerprint while carrying no direct information about mathematical merit. R03 begins with 'Hint', and R07 uses a standard correction template followed by staged algebra.

proposals.name: Markup-display density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how heavily the answer relies on displayed equations, aligned derivations, matrices, tags, and other visible formatting compared with ordinary prose; do not judge whether the formatting improves the mathematics.
proposals.rationale: Formatting habits can be inherited from author practice and can also interact with substantive exposition. R02 contains extensive displayed constructions and a matrix, while R43 is dominated by tagged displays and determinant arrays.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's formatting practice

proposals.name: Uncertainty and self-correction
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for visible hedging, uncertainty, apologies, self-criticism, or explicit admission of an error; do not judge whether the uncertainty is warranted or whether the answer is good.
proposals.rationale: Self-presentation cues can predict how an answer is received without encoding mathematical merit. R04 admits that its result is 'broken', while R18 says the author is 'not sure' and offers qualified alternatives.

proposals.name: Error Locus Precision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer pinpoints exactly which line, step, or expression in the asker's work contains the mistake and explains why it is wrong. Score 0 if the answer makes no reference to any error in the asker's attempt or only says 'this is wrong' without locating the error. Intermediate scores for partial localization.
proposals.rationale: In R55, the answerer identifies the exact sign error ('The error starts at the very beginning') and then completes the corrected derivation. In R59, the answerer quotes the exact line where arithmetic went wrong and provides the corrected expression. The scorecard likely misses how valuable this surgical error-correction is to voters relative to a generic full re-derivation.

proposals.name: Insight-to-Length Economy
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer delivers a crucial, non-obvious mathematical observation in very few words or lines, with essentially no extraneous text. Score 0 if the answer is long but contains low density of actual mathematical insight relative to its length. Judge the ratio of 'key ideas' to total length.
proposals.rationale: R18 is a single algebraic identity ($a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b)$) that immediately resolves the question; R35 reduces the problem to a symmetry observation in three sentences. Both are dense_high despite minimal detail. The scorecard appears to penalize brevity even when the brevity is the point.

proposals.name: Approach Validation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer explicitly confirms that the asker's own method or partial work is fundamentally correct (even if incomplete or containing a minor error), and explains why it works. Score 0 if the answer ignores whether the asker's approach was viable and simply provides an alternative solution.
proposals.rationale: R07 ('Yes. Since Z is free, the sequence splits and you get what you want.') validates the asker's reasoning in one line. R52 ('That looks fine to me') confirms the asker's proof and adds a minor complementary observation. The dense model rewards this confirmation highly; a scorecard measuring completeness or thoroughness would miss it.

proposals.name: Asker-Work Direct Engagement
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer works directly with the asker's notation, specific expressions, or attempted steps, modifying or extending them rather than starting from scratch. Score 0 if the answer presents a fully independent solution with no reference to the asker's particular formulation.
proposals.rationale: R54 corrects the asker's specific derivative line and notation: 'You should have instead (1/xy)(y+xy').' R25 engages with the asker's variable choices ('let y∈φ(G) and g∈G') and shows how to fix the logical setup. This targeted engagement is something a checklist of generic quality dimensions may fail to credit.

proposals.name: Graduated Hint Scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer structures guidance as a clear sequence of buildable sub-steps or questions, each of which the reader can act on independently before proceeding. Score 0 if the answer either dumps a full solution or gives a single unstructured hint with no progression.
proposals.rationale: R02 provides three numbered, sequential hints that build on each other ('Show that... Show that... Apply (1) and (2) twice'). R22 asks the asker a guiding question ('Which terms are that?') after setting up the key observation. The dense model recognizes this pedagogical structure; the scorecard likely scores it low for not providing a complete answer.

proposals.name: Conceptual Confusion Diagnosis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer identifies and names the specific conceptual misunderstanding that led to the question, then explains the correct concept with contrast. Score 0 if the answer addresses only the surface-level computation without diagnosing any underlying confusion.
proposals.rationale: R17 spends the entire answer disentangling two concepts the asker has conflated ('spanning set of V' vs. 'span of a subset of V'), providing formal definitions and a clarifying example. R08 could have just said 'Clairaut's theorem' but instead diagnoses the structural contradiction in the asker's premise. The dense model rewards this diagnostic depth.

proposals.name: Transparent Limitation Acknowledgment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer openly acknowledges that its own method is incomplete, that something is broken, or that the approach has limitations—while still being useful. Score 0 if the answer presents itself as complete and authoritative without acknowledging any gaps or issues.
proposals.rationale: R09 provides a computation and then immediately flags 'this is broken,' which signals intellectual honesty that voters trust. R10 includes a candid editorial opinion ('there's basically no reason to use them anymore... kind of silly') that signals the answerer's expertise. The scorecard may penalize such admissions rather than crediting the transparency.

proposals.name: Analogy Together With Explicit Connection
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer introduces a simpler or parallel mathematical situation AND then explicitly maps the analogy back to the original problem, showing how the parallel resolves the question. Score 0 if no analogy is used, or if an analogy is mentioned without connecting it back.
proposals.rationale: R27 introduces a concrete analogous power series ($\sum x^n = 1/(1-x)$) and then uses it to explain why the region of convergence changes under substitution. R24 uses the idea of 'listing elements' to make cardinality of $\mathbb{N}$ vs. $\mathbb{Z}$ accessible, then connects back to why equipotence is interesting. This bridging work is something the scorecard may not capture.

proposals.name: Systematic Case Decomposition
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer methodically reduces a problem to a small set of cases, eliminates or handles each in turn with clear justification, and reaches a complete conclusion through this structure. Score 0 if the answer handles the problem in an ad hoc manner with no case structure.
proposals.rationale: R16 systematically reduces the problem using modular arithmetic, pruning cases ($a\equiv b$, $a=0$, $a=5$, etc.) with clear modular-arithmetic justifications at each step, eventually reducing to a previously solved case. R30 decomposes the counting problem by parameterizing the number of colored balls and deriving the count for each. The scorecard may not credit the pruning logic itself.

proposals.name: Completeness Calibration to Pedagogical Context
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer provides exactly the right level of detail for the asker's apparent level and the question's nature—leaving appropriate work when the asker is learning, or giving full detail when the asker is stuck on a specific computation. Score 0 if the answer is badly mismatched in either direction: a full solution where a hint would teach more, or a hint when the asker needs a worked example.
proposals.rationale: R30 sets up the summation and then writes 'I leave it you to simplify this expression,' matching the question's level appropriately; the same problem in R51 receives a full derivation including a combinatorial identity proof, which the dense model rates far lower. R11 walks through the long division steps but leaves 'figure out when it becomes periodic' to the asker.

proposals.name: Cross-Method Verification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer confirms its result through two or more genuinely independent mathematical methods or perspectives. Score 0 if only one method or path is used, or if the 'second method' is merely a restatement of the first.
proposals.rationale: R15 derives the recursion formula for the nth derivative and then independently confirms via Taylor expansion, giving the asker two ways to see the answer. R52 confirms via rank arguments and then offers SVD as an alternative perspective. The dense model credits this redundancy as confidence-building; the scorecard may see it as unnecessary.

proposals.name: Meta-Content Contamination (Reverse)
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer is entirely focused on the mathematics with no off-topic digressions, personal asides about other users, formatting requests, or meta-commentary about the answering process. Score 0 if the answer is substantially diluted by content unrelated to the mathematics of the question.
proposals.rationale: R12 ends with '(can somebody please fix up my TeX so the chunk equations is centred and aligned?)' which breaks focus. R33 includes a P.S. explaining which other users needed which computations, and R49 includes extensive meta-commentary about whether the asker already knew the answer. The scorecard may not penalize these dilutions; the dense model appears to.

proposals.name: Exposition Convergence Quality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer has a clear logical arc that builds steadily toward a definite, unambiguous conclusion, with each paragraph advancing the argument. Score 0 if the answer wanders, repeats itself, introduces tangents, or reaches the end without a crisp takeaway.
proposals.rationale: R20 is a long explanation of entropy that circles through encoding cost, Huffman coding, and Shannon's theorem without a clean single thread. R49 is an extremely long answer that includes restatements, parenthetical asides, and self-referential notes that obscure the main argument. In contrast, R14 and R08 each have a single unbroken logical line from setup to conclusion.

proposals.name: Entry-Point Accessibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the very first sentence or mathematical statement of the answer is something the asker can immediately understand or recognize, creating a bridge before any advanced content. Score 0 if the answer opens with formalism or prerequisites that are far above the question's level.
proposals.rationale: R24 opens with 'both sets are of infinite size,' an immediately graspable observation, before introducing cardinality. R35 opens with 'Since |x| = |-x| (more or less by definition),' grounding the argument in something obvious. By contrast, R01 opens with dense algebraic number theory notation that assumes significant background, which may explain why the dense model rates it low.

proposals.name: Difficulty-Level Calibration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the mathematical sophistication of the answer (notation, prerequisites, abstraction level) is well-matched to what the question implies about the asker's background. Score 0 if the answer is dramatically over- or under-sophisticated relative to the question's level.
proposals.rationale: R17 re-explains basic linear algebra definitions (spanning set, span, subspace) at a level matching an introductory course question, earning dense_high. R01 deploys Kummer-Dedekind theorem, Galois theory, and local field methods for what appears to be an introductory algebraic number theory question, earning dense_low despite the card model crediting its thoroughness.

proposals.name: First-person narrative framing
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer uses first-person conversational framing and discursive narration -- phrases like 'Let me give you', 'Let me start by', 'I will describe', 'I think', 'I would do', and extensive storytelling connective tissue around the mathematics. 0 = none, 10 = pervasive. Do NOT judge whether this is good or bad writing.
proposals.rationale: A chatty, self-narrating style reads as substantive to a criterion-based scorecard but may simply reflect author verbosity rather than voter preference. R03 opens 'Let me give you an intuitive interpretation' and narrates at length; R56 is saturated with 'Well, you have already dealt with' and 'I call ... a switch'. Dense-low-card-high items cluster here.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's communicative habit / practice in the format

proposals.name: Cross-reference to other answers or users
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer text explicitly references, attributes, responds to, or builds upon other answers or named users on the same question page (e.g., 'as the other answer notes', 'to expand on Stephen's answer', 'as was pointed out in another answer', '@username'). 0 = no reference at all, 10 = the answer is heavily framed around other answers. Do NOT judge quality.
proposals.rationale: Being a later answer lets one reference predecessors; this is a positional artefact, not quality. R29 opens 'To expand on Stephen's answer'; R54 says 'in Ove Ahlman's answer'; R22 begins 'As was pointed out in another answer'; R06 references two other users by handle.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Non-standard English orthography and grammar
proposals.instruction: Score the extent of non-standard English: missing or extra spaces after punctuation, non-standard spelling, missing articles, informal abbreviations ('U' for 'you', 'r' for 'are'), and grammatical constructions that deviate from standard written English. 0 = standard throughout, 10 = pervasive non-standard English. Do NOT judge whether the English is good or bad, only how much deviates from standard written English.
proposals.rationale: Language background is a pure nuisance -- it affects how models parse text but is irrelevant to voter preference. R52 writes 'U have n black and n white balls' and 'Simplier'; R55 writes 'You mixed them up.If you look' with no space after the period.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's language background

proposals.name: Validation or critique of asker's specific attempt
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer directly engages with, validates, corrects, or comments on the asker's own working, derivation, or stated reasoning (e.g., 'You did it correctly', 'Your error is at line 3', 'You seem to be confused about', 'That looks fine to me'). 0 = no engagement with asker's work, 10 = the answer is entirely structured around correcting or validating the asker's attempt. Do NOT judge whether the engagement is helpful.
proposals.rationale: Addressing the asker personally is a relationship choice, not quality; it may impress a checklist but voters compare answers on merit. R36 says 'You did it correctly ... just made a little arithmetic mistake'; R30 begins 'You are correct except one sign'; R13 opens 'You seem to be greatly confused'; R51 corrects the asker's quantifier logic.
proposals.upstream_parent: answerer's relationship to the reader (writing for the asker vs. future audience)

proposals.name: Flat declarative terseness at answer opening
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer begins with or is dominated by very short, flatly declarative statements, single-word verdicts, or bare hints without any framing or hedging (e.g., 'False.', 'Yes.', 'Hint:', a one-line formula). 0 = answer opens with extended framing, 10 = answer is a bare declarative or hint with no preamble. Do NOT judge whether terseness is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: A terse, declarative register is a marker of an experienced site regular, not of voter preference per se. R04 opens with the single word 'False'; R39 says simply 'Yes.'; R05 is a one-line hint; R46 is a single identity. These items are dense-high but scorecard-low.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's seniority / practice in the format

proposals.name: Dense structured mathematical display
proposals.instruction: Score the extent of heavy structured mathematical formatting: multi-line aligned environments, large matrices, numbered/tagged equations, multi-row derivations using begin/end environments, and systematic display-mode typesetting. 0 = only inline or simple math, 10 = answer is dominated by complex display structures. Do NOT judge whether the formatting is good.
proposals.rationale: Heavy display formatting may impress a scorecard (looks thorough) but is a habit, not a quality signal. R10 uses a large inverse-matrix display; R09 features a multi-row argument matrix and detailed multi-part derivation; R48 has aligned multi-line derivations -- all dense-low-card-high.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's markup habit / practice with site conventions

proposals.name: Total volume of prose explanation
proposals.instruction: Score the total volume of non-mathematical prose in the answer -- the sheer word count of English sentences and connective tissue, excluding mathematical expressions. 0 = almost no prose (nearly all math or one-liners), 10 = very extensive prose. Do NOT judge whether the amount of explanation is good, only how much prose there is.
proposals.rationale: Prose volume is the most basic surface proxy -- a scorecard rewards it, but length is orthogonal to voter preference. R03, R17, and R56 are extremely long prose-heavy answers (all dense-low-card-high), while R02 and R39 are minimal one-liners (dense-high-card-low).
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Meta-commentary and self-referential asides
proposals.instruction: Score the extent of meta-textual commentary: P.S. notes, 'Hope this helps!', edit annotations, formatting requests directed at other users, parenthetical notes explaining the answer itself, and asides about the answering process. 0 = none, 10 = pervasive. Do NOT judge whether these are helpful.
proposals.rationale: Meta-commentary is pure surface noise that a scorecard may read as thoroughness. R06 has a P.S. explaining why computations were added; R17 ends 'Hope this helps!' with an EDIT note; R48 asks 'can somebody please fix up my TeX'; R56 has two signed notes -- all dense-low-card-high.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Pedagogical restatement of basic definitions
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the answer pauses to restate, define, or explain basic concepts or terminology that a reader of the question would plausibly already know -- teaching from scratch rather than answering directly. 0 = no restatement of basics, 10 = extensive restatement. Do NOT judge whether the teaching is good.
proposals.rationale: Restating basics may reflect the question type or answerer's audience choice, not voter preference. R13 devotes multiple paragraphs to defining 'spanning set' and 'span of a subset'; R03 explains encoding and bits from first principles. Both are dense-low-card-high.
proposals.upstream_parent: kind of question the answer is attached to (pedagogical vs. computational)

proposals.name: Informal or non-LaTeX mathematical notation in text
proposals.instruction: Score the extent of informal mathematical notation in the prose: caret symbols for exponents (e.g., t^(3/2)), '>=' or '<=' instead of \geq/\leq, plain-text function names without backslashes (e.g., cot^{-1} without \cot), ASCII arrows (-> instead of \to), and similar. 0 = all math properly typeset, 10 = pervasive informal notation. Do NOT judge whether the notation is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Informal notation is a practice marker orthogonal to quality. R12 writes 'F(t)=(t^(3/2),0,0) where t>=0' entirely in ASCII; R58 uses bare 'cot^{-1}' without \cot and ASCII arrows throughout. Both are dense-low-card-high.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's mathematical writing practice / familiarity with site conventions

proposals.name: Error Localization with Causal Explanation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer pinpoints the exact step, line, or concept where the asker's reasoning breaks down AND explains the mathematical reason it is wrong. Score 0 if no error is identified, or an error is mentioned without any explanation of why it is wrong.
proposals.rationale: The dense model rewards answers that diagnose precisely. R04 identifies the exact conceptual slip ('you have taken arbitrary elements in both the image and in G') and explains the distinction. R38 pinpoints a sign error ('The error starts at the very beginning') and then traces the correction through. In contrast, R10 ('You mixed them up') and R08 ('I'm not sure you can do better') identify problems vaguely with no causal explanation, and the dense model penalizes them.

proposals.name: Insight-to-Length Efficiency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if every sentence carries new mathematical content or a necessary logical connective, with no filler or restatement of standard material. Score 0 if the answer contains extensive text, computation, or repetition that delivers little insight per word.
proposals.rationale: R05 answers the entire question in two sentences containing the key factorisation identity; R43 gives a complete answer in two sentences. The dense model ranks both very high while the scorecard underrates them. Conversely, R01 reproduces a large cofactor matrix and R26 takes many paragraphs to reach a point the dense model apparently finds low-value despite the scorecard's enthusiasm.

proposals.name: Scaffolded Progressive Disclosure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer structures its assistance in ordered stages—each building on the previous—letting the reader participate in the reasoning (e.g., numbered hints, guided questions, incremental setup). Score 0 if it dumps a complete solution with no staging, or gives a single flat statement with no developmental structure.
proposals.rationale: R03 ('Show that… Show that… Apply (1) and (2) twice') and R24 ('Look at the expanded form… Which terms are that?') guide the reader step by step, and the dense model rewards this. R12 and R42 each give a single bare formula or object with no staging, which the dense model penalizes heavily.

proposals.name: Affirm-Then-Correct Pedagogy
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer explicitly acknowledges what the asker did correctly before identifying what needs fixing. Score 0 if it ignores or dismisses the asker's own work entirely.
proposals.rationale: R06 ('You did it correctly. You just made a little arithmetic mistake near the end') and R56 ('That looks fine to me. The other minor piece is…') both validate before correcting, and the dense model ranks them high. R10 ('You mixed them up') and R08 dismiss without any acknowledgment of correct elements, which the dense model penalizes.

proposals.name: Conceptual Root Over Surface Fix
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer addresses the underlying mathematical misconception that caused the error, not merely the surface-level mechanical mistake. Score 0 if it only fixes the mechanics without engaging with the conceptual gap.
proposals.rationale: R31 extensively clarifies the difference between 'spanning set' and 'span of a set,' resolving a deep confusion, and R04 explains why the logical setup is wrong, not just the algebra. The dense model rewards both highly. R14 and R20 apply standard mechanical procedures (substitution, chain rule) without addressing any conceptual understanding, which the dense model ranks low.

proposals.name: Embedded Self-Verification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer includes an explicit correctness check, a second-method confirmation, or an honest acknowledgment of a limitation or gap in its own argument. Score 0 if the answer presents its work with no self-check and no awareness of potential gaps.
proposals.rationale: R15 openly admits 'this is broken' after attempting a method, and R39 confirms its recursion result via Taylor expansion ('This is confirmed by…'). The dense model rewards this intellectual honesty. R57 presents a very long argument with no verification step despite its complexity, and R29 claims 'False' then muddles conditions—both score low in the dense model.

proposals.name: Register-to-Question Calibration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the level of mathematical sophistication, vocabulary, and notation is well-matched to what the question reveals about the asker's background. Score 0 if the answer is drastically too advanced or too elementary for the apparent audience.
proposals.rationale: R02 uses simple factoring for a basic algebra question; R44 patiently explains stem-and-leaf plots at an elementary level. Both are calibrated and ranked high by the dense model. R37 and R57 deploy very heavy machinery for questions that may not demand it, and the dense model ranks them low despite the scorecard's high scores.

proposals.name: Argument Flow and Logical Architecture
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer has a clear logical progression with explicit transitions between steps, making the thread of reasoning easy to follow. Score 0 if the argument is rambling, disjointed, or requires the reader to reconstruct the logical connections.
proposals.rationale: R13 builds a clean proof by contradiction in well-marked stages, and R23 uses systematic case reduction with clear headers. The dense model rewards both. R53 and R57 are very long answers with parenthetical asides, tangents, and edits that disrupt flow, and the dense model ranks them low despite the scorecard rewarding their length and apparent completeness.

proposals.name: Explicit Closure with Question Tie-Back
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer explicitly returns to the original question or goal and states clearly what was shown or concluded. Score 0 if the connection between the answer's content and the original question is left entirely implicit.
proposals.rationale: R17 concludes by tying the inequality back to divergence of the series; R38 ends by reaching the target factorisation explicitly. The dense model rewards this closure. R08 ('I'm not sure you can do better than c(n)=1') and R10 ('You mixed them up') leave the reader without a clear connection back to what was asked.

proposals.name: Notational Discipline and Consistency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if mathematical notation is clean, standard, consistent throughout, and well-formatted. Score 0 if notation is confusing, inconsistent, non-standard, or acknowledged as broken.
proposals.rationale: R38 uses clean aligned equations with a color-coded correction; R39 uses clear recursive notation with explicit definitions. The dense model rewards both. R22 uses informal abbreviations ('U have') and R47 explicitly asks 'can somebody please fix up my TeX,' signaling notational problems the dense model apparently detects.

proposals.name: Transferable Method or Principle
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer teaches a technique, principle, or perspective that applies beyond this specific problem. Score 0 if it only solves this one instance with no generalizable takeaway.
proposals.rationale: R23 teaches modular arithmetic case reduction as a general strategy; R46 explains the general concept of equipotence and different infinities. The dense model rewards both. R14 applies a single mechanical substitution and R42 writes one summation formula—neither conveys a transferable method, and the dense model ranks them low.

proposals.name: Exemplar Selection Quality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if any example, counterexample, or illustration used is minimal, well-chosen, and makes the mathematical point vividly clear. Score 0 if no example is used when one would help, or if the example is poorly chosen and obscures the point.
proposals.rationale: R32 constructs a clean counterexample by extending a formal system with a non-theorem axiom; R41 uses a well-chosen geometric series analogy to illuminate recentering. The dense model rewards both. R12 gives a one-line counterexample 'F(t)=(t^(3/2),0,0)' with zero explanation, and R51 states a counterexample tersely—both score low in the dense model.

proposals.name: Proportional Length-to-Complexity Match
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer's length and depth are well-matched to the complexity and scope of the question—neither over-elaborating a simple question nor under-explaining a hard one. Score 0 if the answer is drastically too long or too short for what the question demands.
proposals.rationale: R05 answers a simple factoring question in two sentences; R52 gives a moderate setup for a combinatorics question. The dense model rewards this proportionality. R01 reproduces an enormous matrix computation, and R53 writes an extremely long answer for a parity puzzle—both are disproportionate, and the dense model ranks them low.

proposals.name: Authentic Engagement and Care Signal
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer conveys genuine interest in helping the asker understand—through encouraging tone, personal touch, or visible effort to be helpful. Score 0 if the tone is perfunctory, dismissive, or robotic.
proposals.rationale: R02 ('Hopefully this shows…') and R06 ('keep doing what you're doing because other than that mistake everything else you wrote is correct') convey warmth and encouragement. The dense model rewards both. R08 ('I'm not sure you can do better') is dismissive, and R10 ('You mixed them up') is curt—both rank low.

proposals.name: Perspective or Approach Diversification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the answer offers a genuinely different angle, method, or framing than the one the asker was attempting, broadening the asker's mathematical toolkit. Score 0 if it only follows the asker's exact path with no alternative viewpoint.
proposals.rationale: R13 uses proof by contradiction when the asker may have sought a direct construction; R23 reframes a combinatorics problem entirely in modular arithmetic. The dense model rewards these fresh perspectives. R20 and R14 apply the standard expected procedure (chain rule, u-substitution) with no alternative framing, and the dense model ranks them low.

proposals.name: Display-math volume share
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer's visual mass is dominated by display-mode (block) mathematical expressions versus running prose. Count both the number of display blocks and their relative footprint. Do NOT judge whether the math is correct, good, or well-chosen; judge only how much of the page is block-level math.
proposals.rationale: The scorecard rewards visible structural density. R02 and R42 are wall-to-wall display math (card_pct 0.874, 1.000) while terse high-dense answers like R13 and R43 are almost all prose (card_pct 0.202, 0.178). Block math reads as 'thorough' to a rubric but is orthogonal to whether voters preferred it.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Terse flat-declarative register
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer uses short, flat, confident declarative sentences with little hedging, little motivational scaffolding, and no self-deprecation. High = punchy expert tone; low = hedged, qualified, or narrative. Do NOT judge whether the tone is good or bad; judge only how terse and declarative the prose is.
proposals.rationale: Practised high-reputation site regulars write this way. R13 ('a²-b²=(a-b)(a+b). If a+b≠0, you can divide...') and R43 ('Yes. Since Z is free, the sequence splits...') are archetype terse-declarative answers scoring dense_pct 0.844/0.785 with very low card_pct. The dense model likely keys on this register as a within-question crowd signal.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice and standing in the format

proposals.name: Explicit cross-reference to other answers or comments
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer text explicitly references, quotes, defers to, corrects, or builds on another specific answer or comment on the same page (e.g. 'as was pointed out in another answer', 'to expand on Stephen's answer', 'I see I've just repeated X's comment'). Do NOT judge whether referencing others is good; score only how much explicit cross-referencing is present.
proposals.rationale: These fingerprints reveal the answer is NOT the first to arrive. R16 ('As was pointed out in another answer'), R26 (quoting Ove Ahlman's answer), R34 ('As in my post'), R38 ('nicely considered in the answer from @ErickWong'), R49 ('To expand on Stephen's answer'), and R59 ('I see I've just repeated Daniel Schepler's comment here') all leak arrival order. First answers cannot reference others, so this channel is a direct position proxy that the dense model may treat as 'derivative' and the card model may miss.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Direct engagement with asker's own work
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer directly quotes, paraphrases, or line-edits the asker's specific derivation or code (e.g. 'You got to here...', 'Your derivative for RHS is correct, but...', 'You did it correctly. You just made a little arithmetic mistake'). Score only visible engagement with the asker's artefact, not whether the engagement is helpful.
proposals.rationale: Answers that diagnose the asker's actual work may earn asker goodwill and votes. R04, R06, R11, R28, R32, and R47 all quote or line-edit the asker's derivation; all are dense_high_card_low. The dense model may read this personalised diagnostic posture as a crowd-preference signal; the card model scores the finished product and misses the engagement.
proposals.upstream_parent: answerer's relationship to the reader (writing for the asker vs future audience)

proposals.name: Meta-discursive and self-referential asides
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer contains non-mathematical meta-discourse: personal opinions about the subject matter, pleas for formatting help, named-dropping of colleagues, postscripts about other users, editorial self-corrections ('edit: this is broken'), or tangential commentary. Do NOT judge whether the asides are useful; score only how much meta-discourse is present.
proposals.rationale: R14 ('kind of silly'), R21 ('can somebody please fix up my TeX'), R22 ('edit: And well, this is broken'), R24 (postscript about user142198 and 'Exam in 5 days'), R44 ('My colleague Chris Cooper...'), and R45 ('I am not 100% sure...') are heavy in meta-discourse. These inflate card scores (they read as 'engaged' or 'thorough') but may depress voter preference; either way they are orthogonal to the target.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Elementary-computation subject signature
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer's mathematical content is at the level of routine single-variable calculus, basic linear algebra, elementary number theory, or high-school algebra (manipulating fractions, solving equations, computing derivatives, etc.). High = unmistakably introductory; low = graduate or research-level. Do NOT judge whether the answer is good for its level.
proposals.rationale: Homework-level questions draw a different and larger voter pool. R03, R05, R12, R13, R15, R18, R53, and R54 are unmistakably elementary; their card scores range high (0.601-0.927) while dense scores are low. The scorecard may reward 'complete-looking' elementary writeups; the dense model is calibrated to within-question preference which behaves differently on mass-traffic elementary threads.
proposals.upstream_parent: kind of question the answer is attached to

proposals.name: Sophisticated LaTeX construct usage
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer uses advanced typesetting constructs: align/cases environments, matrices, colour macros (\color), tagged equations, multi-line derivations with explicit alignment, or custom commands. Simple inline $...$ and single display $$...$$ count low. Do NOT judge whether the formatting aids understanding; score only construct sophistication.
proposals.rationale: R38 uses coloured \color{blue} terms throughout and multi-case alignment (card_pct 0.022 but the construct density is high relative to dense preference), R51 builds a full 3×3 determinant matrix, R11 uses \color{red} for sign correction. Practised users produce richer markup, which the card model may read as 'polished' and the dense model may discount.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's markup habit and format practice

proposals.name: Informal orthography and notation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer exhibits informal or non-standard orthography: SMS-style abbreviations ('U' for 'you'), caret-and-slash math notation in text (t^(3/2), ^3C_1), typos, missing LaTeX delimiters, or ASCII-art mathematics. Do NOT judge whether the informality is bad; score only how much is present.
proposals.rationale: R09 ('U have n black...'), R25 ('F(t)=(t^(3/2),0,0)'), R46 ('switchs', 'firstly at σ'), and R05 (caret-style subscripts in text) carry a first-timer or casual-poster fingerprint. These answers score dense_low but several score card_high (R05 card 0.927, R09 card 0.867), suggesting the card model does not penalise informal orthography while the dense model (tracking voter preference) does.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice and seniority in the format

proposals.name: Hint-and-withhold posture
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer deliberately withholds a full solution and instead gives a 'Hint:', a partial setup, a guiding question, or a roadmap ('Show that...', 'Which terms are that?'). High = the answer stops short of a worked answer by design. Do NOT judge whether hinting is pedagogically good; score only how much is withheld.
proposals.rationale: R08 ('HINT: Work up to it in steps: Show that...'), R30 ('Hint: ... Which terms are that?'), R53, R54, R55 ('Hint: Complete the square... Answer: 13.'), and R58 are explicit hint answers. Voters on math.SE have a documented preference for hint answers on homework-style questions; the dense model captures this, the card model (which credits completeness) systematically under-scores it (R08 card 0.344, R30 card 0.293, R55 card 0.272).
proposals.upstream_parent: answerer's relationship to the reader (teaching posture)

proposals.name: Narrative motivational scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the answer wraps its mathematics in extended verbal motivation: framing analogies ('the cost of encoding...', 'captain and his team'), 'let me explain', 'intuitively', discursive hand-holding, or multi-paragraph verbal scene-setting before or between equations. Do NOT judge whether the scaffolding helps; score only how much extended motivational prose is present.
proposals.rationale: R23 ('One immediate (though rather dangerous!) way to wrap your mind around...'), R31 ('An engineering explanation: say you have a sampling grid...'), R52 ('Let me give you an intuitive... interpretation...'), and R09 (verbal 'captain' analogy) are heavy on narrative scaffolding. These inflate card scores (R31 card 0.932, R52 card 0.825) but the dense model reads them as length without proportional voter preference, producing the disagreement.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience the answerer is writing for (asker vs future searchers)
